commitResults.messageTitle: Document the branch naming convention in AGENTS.md
commitResults.messageBody:
The Git conventions section of AGENTS.md covers commit message subjects
and bodies, but says nothing about branch names, although the se-edu
conventions it links to prescribe those too. Contributors have to follow
the link to find out how to name a branch, and it is easy to assume the
conventions govern issue titles and descriptions as well, which they do
not.

Let's record the branch naming rules alongside the commit message rules,
and state that the conventions stop at commit messages and branch names.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document the branch lifecycle rules in AGENTS.md
commitResults.messageBody:
The Git conventions section of AGENTS.md links only to the se-edu
conventions, which say nothing about what happens to a branch after its
PR merges. Admin Appendix E adds two rules of its own: branches must
survive the merge, and branches are synced by merging rather than
rebasing. Both exist because the course scripts read branches and commit
timestamps, so breaking either costs marks in a way that is invisible
from the diff.

Let's record both rules next to the branch naming convention, and note
that they come from the course admin pages rather than from se-edu.

commitResults.messageTitle: Rename AB3 packages and classes to TAB
commitResults.messageBody:
The codebase carries the names of the sample project it was forked
from: the root package is seedu.address, the model root is AddressBook,
and the entity every command operates on is Person. Our product is a
teaching assistant's student book, so every one of those names tells a
reader something untrue, and the mismatch grows more expensive the more
feature code we add on top of it.

Let's rename the root package to seedu.tab, AddressBook to StudentBook
and Person to Student, along with the files, packages, test fixtures and
data files named after them. Address stays, since it remains a field on
a student. The documentation is renamed separately.

commitResults.messageTitle: Close sub-issues when their parent is closed
commitResults.messageBody:
The issue tracker records each MVP feature as an epic with its user
stories linked beneath it. GitHub does not cascade a close down that
hierarchy, so closing an epic leaves every story under it open. The
tracker then shows work outstanding that is done, and the v1.2 burndown
reads wrong.

Let's add a workflow that closes the open sub-issues of any issue that
is closed, leaving a comment on each saying which parent closed it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Update the target user profile and value prop
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide describes a user who has a need to manage a
significant number of contacts, and offers them contact management
faster than a mouse-driven GUI. That is AB3's audience and AB3's pitch,
so a reader of our own guide learns nothing about who TAB is for or why
they would pick it over a spreadsheet.

Let's replace both with the profile and value proposition the team
settled on: an NUS School of Computing teaching assistant running 2 to 3
tutorial or lab slots a semester, and a semester of students managed
faster than a spreadsheet or a mouse-driven contact app.

commitResults.messageBody:

the section documents the requirements of the project we forked rather

Let's replace them with the sixty stories the team gathered, each with a

commitResults.messageTitle: Point AGENTS.md at the renamed packages
commitResults.messageBody:
AGENTS.md is the first file a contributor or an agent reads to orient
itself in this repository, and five of its pointers lead nowhere: the
main class, the source and test roots, the jar name and the test-utility
path all still name seedu.address, which the rename to seedu.tab
removed. It also calls docs/ a Jekyll site, which the move to MarkBind
ended.

Let's point all of them at what the repository holds.

commitResults.messageTitle: Accept names that real students have
commitResults.messageBody:
Name rejects anything outside letters, digits and spaces, so a teaching
assistant cannot record Ravi s/o Kumaran, Siti Nur-Aisyah, Sean O'Brien
or Ma Ying-jeou, nor any name written in a non-Latin script. Those names
are on the roster, and the slash is rejected only because the parser
happens to use it as a delimiter. The PE bug guidelines name this exact
case as a feature flaw.

Let's accept any name that carries an identity, requiring only that it
holds at least one letter or number and neither begins nor ends with
whitespace, judged against the whole of Unicode rather than ASCII. Four
fixtures encoded the old rule and no longer describe an invalid name, so
they move to a value that still is one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Store names in a normalized form
commitResults.messageBody:
A name is not only displayed. The search splits it into words on ASCII
whitespace, and isSameStudent compares it as the identity of a student.
The widened rule admits names that defeat both: John<NBSP>Doe cannot be
found by searching for John, and a leading zero-width space produces a
second student indistinguishable from the first. The review of #83
reproduced both, and the Developer Guide's claim that a name is never
parsed nor compared was wrong.

Let's normalize a name as it is constructed, composing it to NFC,
discarding the zero-width space and byte order mark, reducing runs of
any Unicode whitespace to one ASCII space and trimming the ends. The
joiner and non-joiner stay, because Sinhala and Arabic need them. The
rest of the application can then keep its ASCII assumption, and names
that look identical compare equal.

Surrounding whitespace is trimmed rather than rejected, which is what
the feature specification asks for. VALIDATION_REGEX described only half
the rule, so it gives way to two named patterns. AddCommandParserTest
covers the names end to end and pins the one the prefix syntax still
rejects, and both guides record the rule.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name: Widen the message and the whitespace tests
commitResults.messageBody:
Review of #83 raises two points. The constraint message says a name
needs a letter or a number, which reads oddly for a logographic script:
a reader with a Chinese name is told to supply a letter. The whitespace
tests cover only the space character, although the rule spans every kind
of Unicode whitespace.

Let's say letter, character or number, from any writing system, and
cover the tab, the line feed, the carriage return, the form feed, the
vertical tab, the em and thin spaces, the ogham space mark and the
ideographic space that a CJK input method produces.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the fields an add command leaves out
commitResults.messageBody:
Leaving a field out of an add command prints the whole usage block,
including the example, and never says which field is missing. The user
has to compare their command against the example to find out. The PE bug
triaging guidelines call this out: an error message can be correct yet
give too many possible reasons without pointing at the specific one.

Only the first missing field would be worth naming if the parser stopped
at one, so it collects them all.

Let's have a prefix carry the name of the field it marks, and report the
fields that are missing rather than the format of the whole command.
Text before the first prefix is left alone: that is a malformed command
rather than an omitted field, and it keeps the usage block.

commitResults.messageTitle: MessagesTest: Cover the preconditions of both methods
commitResults.messageBody:
Codecov reports a partial branch on the assertion that guards
getErrorMessageForMissingPrefixes against being called with no prefixes.
The assertion is right, because a message that names no field at all
leaves the user with a colon and nothing after it, so the branch wants a
test rather than removal.

The method beside it carries the same assertion and has never had a test
of its own, and MessagesTest is a new file, so it may as well describe
the whole class.

Let's assert that each of the two rejects an empty call, and that the
older of them formats a single prefix as it always has.

commitResults.messageTitle: Read the field labels from the prefixes that own them
commitResults.messageBody:
Review of #85 raises three points.

The missing-field tests append a raw value where a prefix was dropped,
so the name under test also absorbs a stray number and each case fails
for two reasons at once. No case omits the name at all.

A field label such as NAME is now written twice, once where the prefix
is declared and again in the usage text of add and edit, so a rename
would leave the usage and the missing-field error disagreeing.

A test named for equals also asserts on hashCode.

Let's omit a field cleanly in each test and add the missing name, build
the usage text from the labels the prefixes carry, and give hashCode a
test of its own.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say what is wrong with a rejected value
commitResults.messageBody:
A value that fails validation is answered with the whole rule for its
field and no mention of what was typed. An email missing its @ earns
eight lines of specification, none of which say which character is
absent or quote the value. The PE bug triaging guidelines treat an
error message that gives too many possible reasons without pointing at
the specific one as a feature flaw.

Let's quote the value and give the reason. Each value class explains why
it turned a particular string down, and the parser composes that into
one line naming the field. Email distinguishes a missing at sign from a
doubled one, an empty local part, an empty domain, a malformed local
part and a final domain label shorter than two characters.

The full rule stays where someone looking for the format will read it,
and the data file keeps its own messages, since a reader repairing JSON
by hand wants the rule rather than a single value.

commitResults.messageTitle: Accept the tags and phone numbers a roster holds
commitResults.messageBody:
A tag must match \p{Alnum}+, so Lab 3, Tutorial 5 and needs-followup are
all rejected, along with every tag in a non-Latin script. Those are the
tags the week 7 specification lists as valid parameters, and Lab 3 and
needs-followup are printed in docs/images/Ui.png. Week 5 records that
students are sliced by slot, module, semester, project team and status;
three of those five forms cannot be typed.

A phone number must match \d{3,}, so +65 9123 4567 is rejected, which is
how week 5 records that this user stores numbers. The PE bug triaging
guidelines use that case as their own example of overzealous validation.

Let's let both hold what a roster holds, asking only that a tag carries
a letter or a number and that a phone number carries three digits.
Neither is parsed, dialled or used to build a path, so no character in
either can hinder the app.

Name already stored a normalized form for the same reason, and a tag is
a key in a set, so the normalizer moves to StringUtil and all three
share it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'master' into 84-explain-the-rejected-value
Compose a field value after deleting from it
commitResults.messageBody:
Review of #86 finds three faults.

A zero-width character between a base letter and its combining mark
blocks the two from composing, and the normalizer composes before it
deletes. So "e" with a zero-width space and a combining acute is stored
as a decomposed pair, unequal to the single character it looks like, and
the search misses it. The fault reaches tags as well as names.

The reason given for a rejected name or tag says it holds no letter,
character or number, of a value such as --- that plainly holds
characters. A change made to give accurate reasons cannot itself
mislead.

The Developer Guide gives one rationale to three fields that do not
share it. Only a name is searched, and a phone number is neither an
identity nor a key in a set.

Let's delete first and compose last, say letter or number, and describe
each field by what is actually true of it. The method is renamed to
normalizeFieldValue, since it does more than whitespace, and a storage
test proves a phone number with a country code and a tag with a space
survive a save and a load.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the field and the domain length once each
commitResults.messageBody:
Review of #86 asks about two literals.

ParserUtil writes the name of each field as a string where it composes
the message, so five names sit apart from the classes they describe and
nothing keeps them spelled the same way.

Email writes 2 twice, once in the regex for the last domain label and
once in the sentence that explains it, so the two can drift apart.

Let's give each value class the name it is reported under, and Email a
constant for the shortest last label it accepts.

commitResults.messageBody: Explain rejected values, and stop rejecting valid ones

commitResults.messageTitle: Report every fault in an add command at once
commitResults.messageBody:
The parser refuses a command at the first field it cannot accept, so a
user who mistyped the phone and the email is told about the phone,
corrects it, and only then learns about the email. Week 5 records the
complaint: supply a bad phone and a bad email and you round-trip twice.
A missing field and a bad value are reported separately for the same
reason, so leaving out the email while mistyping the phone also takes
two attempts.

Let's examine every field before refusing, and list what is wrong with
each on its own line. A field the command left out is reported once, as
missing, rather than again as a value that cannot be read.

ParseProblems holds the faults found so far and decides at the end
whether to stop, which keeps the parser reading as a list of fields
rather than as a chain of conditionals.

commitResults.messageTitle: Collect every bad tag, and bound the claim
commitResults.messageBody:
Review of #89 finds that the claim overreaches. A value before the first
prefix and a single-valued prefix given twice are both refused before
any field is read, and parseTags stops at the first tag it cannot
accept, so a command with two bad tags reports one.

The first two are not faults in a field. Until it is settled which value
belongs to which field, there is nothing to say about any of them, so
each is refused on its own. The third is the very fault this change
exists to remove and had simply been missed.

Let's parse each tag separately so that every bad one is reported, and
say in the guide and in the parser that fields are collected once the
shape of the command is settled, rather than claiming every mistake is
always gathered.

commitResults.messageTitle: Remove the cancelled address field
commitResults.messageBody:
TAB-131 is marked cancelled in the story sheet and sits among the
stories the Developer Guide records as dropped, yet add still refuses a
command without an address. A teaching assistant therefore invents one
for every student, which is the thing TAB-125 exists to prevent for
email.

Let's take the field out of the student, the commands, the storage, the
card and the sample data.

Two consequences beyond the deletion. The a/ prefix goes with it, and
that prefix was what read a/l and a/p in a Malaysian name as the start
of another field, so those names now parse. And every data file written
so far holds an address key, which must keep loading; a fixture in that
older shape proves it does.

commitResults.messageTitle: StudentTest: Cover the hash of a student
commitResults.messageBody:
Codecov reports hashCode as uncovered. It is uncovered on master too,
and only reaches the patch because removing the address field changed
the line. Nothing has ever called it: a student is held in a list rather
than a hashed collection, so the method has no exercise.

Let's assert the contract, that two students which compare equal hash
alike, and that each remaining field reaches the hash.

commitResults.messageTitle: Take the address out of the guide and the diagrams
commitResults.messageBody:
Review of #91 finds the field still in three places.

The User Guide hands out four commands that hold an a/ fragment. With
the prefix gone the fragment joins the value before it, so the Betsy
example now fails on its email, and the example meant to show a phone
error never reaches the phone.

Both model diagrams still declare Address and draw the student pointing
at it, of a class the same change deletes.

The test for a file in the older shape checked three fields while the
description claimed the student loaded intact. Comparing the whole
student shows the claim was wrong for a different reason: the fixture
spelled the tag key tagged rather than tags, so the tag was dropped and
the narrower assertion passed anyway.

Let's correct the guide, the two diagrams and the fixture, compare the
whole student, and clear the comments and blank gaps the deletions left.

commitResults.messageTitle: Close the gaps a removed call left mid-chain
commitResults.messageBody:
Review of #91 finds two blank lines sitting inside a builder chain,
where the call that set the address used to be.

Let's close them.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge pull request #91 from dillionlim/90-remove-the-address-field
commitResults.messageBody: Remove the cancelled address field

commitResults.messageTitle: Let a student be recorded without an email
commitResults.messageBody:
A teaching assistant meets a student, has a phone number and nothing
else, and cannot record them: add refuses the command without an
email, so an address gets invented to satisfy it. TAB-125 asks for the
opposite, that partial details be recorded as partial.

Let's hold the email as absent rather than as a made-up value. A
student keeps it as null and hands it out as an Optional, so a caller
has to decide what to do when there is none rather than meeting one by
accident. The card leaves its row out, the result box omits the field,
and a saved file simply carries no email key.

A file that holds an email keeps being checked: an address that is
present and malformed is still refused rather than quietly dropped.

commitResults.messageTitle: Record in both guides that the email is optional
commitResults.messageBody:
The User Guide gives add a format where the email is required, and the
Developer Guide describes three fields that must each hold something.
Neither now matches the command.

Let's mark the field optional in the format and the summary, say that
an email cannot be cleared once set, and record why the field is
nullable rather than an Optional.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test the student card on a headless toolkit
commitResults.messageBody:
The card decides whether to show an email and now has a branch that
nothing exercises. It cannot be tested as the project stands: building
one needs the JavaFX toolkit started, and a CI runner has no display,
so the class has never been covered at all.

Let's give the test task a headless toolkit through Monocle and cover
the card: an email that is present reaches the label, one that is absent
leaves the row out rather than leaving it blank, and the tags appear in
order.

StudentBuilder takes a null email, since a student without one is now
an ordinary student rather than an impossible one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Match the headless toolkit to the JavaFX version
commitResults.messageBody:
Platform.startup throws a NullPointerException on the runners. The
headless toolkit is version 21 while JavaFX here is 17, and the two
disagree about the native library the toolkit loads.

Let's take the toolkit at the version JavaFX is at, and drop the
properties that belong to a test robot this project does not use.

commitResults.messageTitle: Drop the headless toolkit from the test task
commitResults.messageBody:
The test task starts a Monocle toolkit so that the student card, and
the branch that decides whether to show an email, can be covered.
Monocle fails to start on every CI runner with a NullPointerException
out of Platform.startup, on both the 21.0.2 and the 17.0.10 release,
while the same run passes headless on a development machine. The build
therefore fails on ubuntu, macos and windows for a reason that has
nothing to do with the change under review.

Let's take the toolkit and the card test back out, so this branch is
judged on the optional email alone. A JavaFX test harness is worth
having, but it changes the build for every contributor and belongs in
a pull request the team weighs on its own merits.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give the storage test a real email to work with
commitResults.messageBody:
VALID_EMAIL in JsonAdaptedStudentTest reads BENSON.getEmail() and calls
toString on the result. That getter hands back an Optional, so the
constant holds the wrapper's text rather than johnd@example.com, and no
validator would accept it. Every test that passes the constant asserts
on a name, phone or tag fault that is raised before the email is looked
at, so they all pass without noticing.

Let's unwrap the Optional, and add a test that builds a student from
VALID_EMAIL and expects the address to survive, so a constant that
stops being an email is caught. The invalid-email test that repeats its
neighbour word for word goes with it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Leave build.gradle as this branch found it
commitResults.messageBody:
Taking the Monocle toolkit back out of the test task leaves behind the
blank line that its system properties sat under. That line is the only
mark the branch makes on build.gradle, so the file joins the diff
carrying nothing a reviewer can act on.

Let's remove it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Leave the email out of a saved file
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide says a saved file carries no email key for a student
who has none. Jackson writes every field it is handed, so the file holds
an email set to null instead. Anyone opening the file by hand meets a
schema the guide does not describe, and a null is an awkward thing to
ask a reader to edit around.

Let's have the adapted student drop a null field, and test that a
student without an email survives a save and a reload with no key
written. StudentBuilder gains a spelling for such a student, which the
tests here and the ones after it need.

commitResults.messageTitle: Stop presenting the email as required
commitResults.messageBody:
Three places still say that every student has an email. The add
command's usage text lists the email prefix unbracketed, so a user who
mistypes the command is told to supply one. The User Guide shows a
refusal naming the email among the missing fields, which the parser no
longer hands back. The Student class promises that its details are
present and not null, which its own constructor contradicts.

Let's bracket the prefix, replace the example with a refusal the parser
does produce, and have the class say what the constructor already does.

commitResults.messageTitle: Cover the student who has no email
commitResults.messageBody:
The suite holds no student without an email, so the state this change
exists to allow goes untested. Adding one, editing another of their
fields, giving them an email later, and comparing two of them all run
against fixtures that carry one, and a regression in the feature would
pass the suite.

Let's test each of those, so that an email that quietly reappears or
goes missing is caught.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give the Linux CI job a display
commitResults.messageBody:
The macOS and Windows runners carry a desktop session, so JavaFX starts
a toolkit there and a test may build a UI node. The Linux runner has
none, and GtkApplication refuses with "Unable to open DISPLAY", so a
test that touches the UI passes on two platforms out of three. The
Linux job is also the one that uploads coverage, so the UI classes can
never be reported as covered.

Let's run a virtual display on that job, so every platform can exercise
the UI classes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test the student card
commitResults.messageBody:
The card decides whether to show an email, and nothing exercises either
branch. The class has no test at all, so the row that a student without
an email is meant to leave out is checked only by eye.

Let's cover the card: an email that is present reaches the label, one
that is absent leaves the row unmanaged rather than blank, a name and
phone carrying symbols arrive as given, and the tags are shown in
order.

commitResults.messageTitle: Load a hand-edited file that spells no email
commitResults.messageBody:
The tests reach an absent email by handing the adapted student a Java
null, which skips Jackson and the storage layer entirely. A file edited
by hand is where an absent email really arrives, and it may spell one
two ways: the key set to null, or the key left out. Neither is read by
any test, though this change alters what the file is allowed to hold.

Let's add a fixture holding both spellings and load it through storage,
so a student who has no email survives the trip from disk.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say that the email is optional where it is described
commitResults.messageBody:
The model diagrams draw an unqualified line from a student to an email,
which reads as one the student must have. The card explains that it
hides the row to avoid a gap "where the address used to be", naming a
field the project no longer holds. The add parser says that an absent
prefix is already reported as missing, which stopped being true when
the email became optional.

Let's mark the email end of the diagrams as 0..1 and correct both
comments.

commitResults.messageTitle: Pin the text of a result that has no email
commitResults.messageBody:
Messages.format leaves the email out for a student who has none. The
tests that exercise it build their expected result by calling format
itself, so they agree with whatever it produces and would not notice
"Email: null", a separator left behind, or another field dropped.

Let's assert the whole string for a student with an email, one without,
and one with neither an email nor a tag.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a tokenizer for quoted command arguments
commitResults.messageBody:
The add command reads its fields from the n/ p/ e/ t/ prefixes, which a
value cannot itself hold: a name carrying p/ followed by a space is
read as the start of another field. The syntax that replaces them marks
fields with flags and takes the name as a positional value, and nothing
can be read from the arguments until they are split into tokens.

Let's add a tokenizer that splits on whitespace and lets double quotes
group a value holding spaces, or one opening with the hyphen that marks
a flag. A token remembers whether quotes took part in it, since that is
the only thing telling "-Ahmad" apart from an option. A quote left open
is reported as such, rather than surfacing later as a malformed field.

commitResults.messageTitle: Read a command as a name followed by flags
commitResults.messageBody:
A field marked by a prefix cannot appear inside a value, and a name is
exactly where such characters turn up: s/o survives only because no
field is marked s/, and a/l did not survive at all until the address
field was removed. Marking fields with flags and taking the name first
avoids the collision, but nothing can read that shape.

Let's add a reader for it over the tokenizer. The tokens before the
first flag are the name, each flag takes the token after it, and a flag
may repeat where the field allows it. An unknown flag, a flag left
without a value, and a token belonging to no flag are each reported for
what they are. No command uses it yet.

commitResults.messageTitle: Take the fields of add as options
commitResults.messageBody:
A prefix has to be a sequence that a value never contains, and no such
sequence exists for a name. s/o, d/o, a/l and a/p are ordinary parts of
Singaporean and Malaysian names, and a/l was unreadable for as long as
the address field was marked a/. Widening the prefixes moves the
collision rather than removing it.

Let's read add as a name followed by options, NAME -p PHONE [-e EMAIL]
[-t TAG]..., so that a value is a whole token and a name is read as a
name however it is spelled. A value that holds spaces, or opens with
the option marker, goes in double quotes.

edit keeps its prefixes for now. Its fields are all optional and it has
no positional value to protect, so it gains nothing from the change.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document how add reads its arguments
commitResults.messageBody:
The guides describe add as taking prefixes, down to the warning that a
name holding p/ is unreadable, which the new syntax removes. Nothing
records why the command reads differently from the rest either.

Let's rewrite the add section of the User Guide, say in the notes that
the two spellings exist side by side, and explain the two parsing
passes and the reason for them in the Developer Guide. A test reads the
worked examples back out of the User Guide and parses each one, since a
guide handing out a command the app refuses is a bug whichever of the
two is wrong.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test the flag type and the messages about flags
commitResults.messageBody:
Flag carries the equality that lets a map find the values given for a
field, and the two new message helpers each hold a precondition, yet
none of them is reached by a test. A lone hyphen decides whether a
token marks a field, and nothing gives it one either.

Let's test Flag the way Prefix is already tested, assert both new
messages including the precondition they carry, and give the tokenizer
a hyphen standing on its own.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep the new parser classes from being instantiated
commitResults.messageBody:
CliFlags, CommandTokenizer and FlagTokenizer hold only static members,
so the compiler gives each a public constructor that means nothing. A
reader may reasonably build one and find it useless, and the coverage
report counts a constructor nobody calls against the change.

Let's make each constructor private. JaCoCo leaves out an empty private
constructor in a class of static members, so the three classes report
as fully covered, which they are.

The three parser classes that came before them still carry the implicit
constructor. Giving them the same treatment belongs in its own change.

commitResults.messageTitle: Read an option in the value position as a missing value
commitResults.messageBody:
An option takes whatever token follows it, without asking what that
token is. So `add John -p 123 -t -e` stores "-e" as a tag and reports
nothing, and `add John -p -e john@example.com` takes "-e" as the phone
and then complains about the address instead of the empty phone. Both
are plain mistakes, and both are read as something the user did not
write.

Let's treat an unquoted option where a value belongs as the option
before it having been left empty, and say which field needs the value.
A value that really does open with a hyphen is given in quotes, so the
message says so.

commitResults.messageTitle: Let a value hold a quote or a backslash
commitResults.messageBody:
A double quote is syntax with no way to escape it, so it is stripped
wherever it appears: `add Dwayne "The Rock" Johnson` stores the name
without its quotes and says nothing. Name accepts any punctuation as
long as a letter or number remains, and a tag may hold a quote too, so
the tokenizer silently discards characters the fields allow.

Let's read a backslash before a quote or another backslash as that
character. A backslash before anything else stays where it is, so a
value gains no new way to lose characters.

commitResults.messageTitle: Record that edit still collides with its prefixes
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide says edit gains nothing from options. It does: the
collision the options remove from add is still there, and `edit 1
n/John p/ Smith` reads Smith as a phone number, so a name add accepts
cannot be typed into edit at all. Two commands reading differently is a
second problem on top of that one. The usage text and the Prefix
javadoc also describe the syntax wrongly, and an undo diagram shows a
command that no longer parses.

Let's say what the limitation is in both guides, warn the reader of the
User Guide where edit is described, point at issue #105 for converting
it, and correct the three stale descriptions.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge pull request #104 from jxinnan/add-pr-review-guidelines
commitResults.messageBody: Add PR review guidelines to AGENTS.md

commitResults.messageTitle: Call the value before the options a preamble
commitResults.messageBody:
FlagArgumentMap and FlagTokenizer sit beside ArgumentMultimap as the
shared way to read a command, yet they call the value before the first
option a name. Only add reads it as a name. edit, which issue #105 is
about converting, would read an index there, and would have to ask for
getName to get one.

Let's call it the preamble, the word ArgumentMultimap already uses for
the same position, and leave the label NAME with the command that takes
a name.

commitResults.messageTitle: Tidy the parser internals a reviewer walked through
commitResults.messageBody:
A few things read worse than they work. Two flags sharing a marker
throw out of the collector rather than being read as one field. put
takes the defensive copy that getAllValues makes for its callers,
mutates it, and puts it back. The duplicate-field message collects into
a set, so the fields can be named in a different order from one run to
the next. One assertion compares a boolean against true.

Let's merge duplicate markers, build the list in place, keep the order
the fields were given in, and assert the boolean directly.

commitResults.messageTitle: Answer a stray value without guessing why it is there
commitResults.messageBody:
The message for a value belonging to no option says a name holding
spaces needs quotes. That is one cause out of several and wrong about
the rest: a quoted name given after the options is already quoted, a
second tag written without repeating the option is not a name, and a
value left over from a typing slip is neither. The tokenizer still
documents that a quote cannot appear in a value, which stopped being
true when the escape was added, and the tip that teaches quoting uses a
name holding a slash, which needs no quotes at all.

Let's state the three rules a stray value can break rather than naming
one cause, and correct every description of the quoting rule that says
more than it should.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say preamble in the summary as well as the body
commitResults.messageBody:
FlagTokenizer's class javadoc opens by saying it reads a name followed
by flagged fields, while the paragraph under it says preamble. The
rename reached the paragraph and not the sentence above it, so the
class contradicts itself on the first line a reader meets. The same
sentence about a value opening with the flag marker calls it a name.

Let's finish the rename in both places.

commitResults.messageTitle: Split a command on a pasted non-breaking space
commitResults.messageBody:
The tokenizer splits on Character.isWhitespace, which leaves out the
non-breaking space. A field value is normalized with a pattern that
does match it, so the two disagree about what separates one value from
the next, and the disagreement is invisible until it bites.

A command pasted from a web page or a chat message carries non-breaking
spaces. One between a name and an option reports the phone as missing
while "-p 91234567" sits plainly in the command, and one after an
option reports that there is no "-p 91234567" option. Both read as the
app failing to see what the user typed.

Let's put the decision in StringUtil beside the pattern that normalizes
a field, and have the tokenizer ask it, so the two cannot drift apart
again. The ideographic space a Chinese keyboard produces is covered by
the same change.

commitResults.messageTitle: Take the whitespace rule from the pattern itself
commitResults.messageBody:
isWhitespace names the characters that separate one value from the
next, and its javadoc claims that this keeps it agreeing with the
pattern normalizeFieldValue collapses with. It does not. U+0085 is
matched by the pattern and by neither Character method, and U+001C is
claimed by Character and not by the pattern, so the two disagree in
both directions. Naming the characters was the same mistake as having
two definitions, only harder to see.

Let's ask the pattern rather than restate it, and check every value a
char can hold against it, so the agreement is a fact rather than a
claim. The cost is a small string per character of a typed command,
which no user will notice.

commitResults.messageTitle: Ask the one whitespace pattern there is
commitResults.messageBody:
isWhitespace matches against a second pattern spelling the same rule as
the one normalizeFieldValue collapses with. Two patterns that have to
stay identical are the drift the method was written to remove, moved
one line further down.

Let's use the pattern already there. Matching one or more whitespace
characters against a single character is the same as matching one, and
the agreement is then with the pattern itself rather than with a copy
of it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge pull request #126 from jxinnan/66-add-follow-up-flag
commitResults.messageBody: Add student follow-up flag

commitResults.messageTitle: Separate a command word on any Unicode whitespace
commitResults.messageBody:
The tokenizer splits arguments on any Unicode whitespace, so that a
command pasted from a web page or a chat message works. The split
before it does not. StudentBookParser matches an ASCII-oriented
pattern against a trimmed input, and three things go wrong: \S without
the Unicode flag treats only ASCII whitespace as a separator, trim
removes nothing above U+0020, and a dot that is not DOTALL refuses an
input holding a line terminator.

Twenty-one of the twenty-five characters the tokenizer accepts fail
here, so "add John -p 91234567" typed with a non-breaking space is
answered with "Unknown command." and no hint of what is wrong with a
command that looks right on screen.

Let's ask StringUtil, which is where the rule lives, and drop the
pattern rather than correct it. Writing the rule a second time is what
produced this, and a test now walks every value a char can hold to
prove the two agree.

commitResults.messageTitle: Hand the arguments on without the separator
commitResults.messageBody:
Starting the arguments at the separator leaves it as their first
character. The add command survives that, because its tokenizer knows
every Unicode separator, and the others do not: delete reads an index
that is not a number, edit finds no prefix, and find quietly searches
for a keyword nobody typed. Only six of the twenty-five separators
leave delete and edit working.

The sweep added with the boundary fix walks only the add command, so
it reports every separator working while three commands are broken.

Let's hand on whatever separated the two as a single space, so that a
command means the same thing whichever one was typed, and compare each
separator against a space across delete, edit, find and add rather
than asking only whether a command came back.

commitResults.messageTitle: Unicode whitespace is not accepted between a command word and its arguments #129 (#130)
commitResults.messageBody:
The tokenizer splits arguments on any Unicode whitespace, so that a
command pasted from a web page or a chat message works. The split
before it did not, and 21 of the 25 separators it accepts were refused
as an unknown command.

Let's ask StringUtil, where the rule already lives, and hand whatever
separated the command word from its arguments on as a single space, so
that a command means the same thing whichever one was typed.

commitResults.messageTitle: ParseProblems: Add optional and repeated field helpers
commitResults.messageBody:
AddCommandParser holds two private helpers beside its own parsing:
parseIfPresent, which parses the value of a flag that may be absent,
and parseEachTag, which parses every value of a repeatable flag and
keeps the ones accepted. Neither is specific to add. EditCommandParser
needs both once it reads options rather than prefixes, so each would
have to be copied across, leaving two places to fix whenever the way a
field is collected changes.

Let's move them onto ParseProblems as collectIfPresent and collectEach,
which is where collect already lives, and have AddCommandParser call
them. Both take an Optional or a Collection rather than a
FlagArgumentMap, so ParseProblems stays independent of how a command's
arguments were tokenized.

commitResults.messageTitle: CommandTestUtil: Drop ADD_ from option fixtures
commitResults.messageBody:
CommandTestUtil holds two sets of field fixtures: NAME_DESC_AMY and its
siblings spell a field the way edit reads it, with a prefix, and
ADD_NAME_AMY and its siblings spell the same field the way add reads
it, with an option. The ADD_ part of the second set exists only to tell
the two apart. Once edit takes options as well there is one spelling,
and the prefix reads as though the fixtures belonged to add alone
rather than to every command.

Let's drop ADD_ from that set, leaving ADD_NAME_AMY as NAME_AMY and so
on. This is a rename of the thirteen constants and their references in
AddCommandParserTest and LogicManagerTest, reproducible by substituting
ADD_ with nothing before each of their names, together with the import
reordering Checkstyle then asks for.

commitResults.messageTitle: Take the fields of edit as options
commitResults.messageBody:
edit marks each field with a prefix: edit 1 n/John p/ Smith stores
"Smith" as the phone number, because a prefix has to be a sequence a
value never contains and no such sequence exists for a name. A name that
add accepts therefore cannot be typed into edit at all, and the only way
to correct one is to delete the student and add them again. The two
commands also read differently, so a user has to remember which of
add John -p 98765432 and edit 1 p/98765432 belongs to which command.

Let's give edit the same options add takes,
edit INDEX [-n NAME] [-p PHONE] [-e EMAIL] [-t TAG]... [--follow-up],
reusing CommandTokenizer and FlagTokenizer. An option is a whole token,
so a value is read as a value however it is spelled.

Clearing the tags moves from a bare t/ to an explicitly empty -t "",
since a bare option is an error: it is how edit 1 -t -e a@b.com reports
the empty -t rather than storing "-e" as a tag. --follow-up still
toggles, as f/ did; setting and clearing it explicitly is issue #146.

The index is read where add reads the name, so a mistyped index now
joins the field problems rather than printing the whole format, and a
command with several mistakes reports them together.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document edit's options in the User Guide
commitResults.messageBody:
The User Guide gives edit's format as
edit INDEX [n/NAME] [p/PHONE_NUMBER] [e/EMAIL] [t/TAG]... [f/], carries
a Known limitation box saying a name holding a prefix cannot be typed
into edit, and tells the reader that add and edit mark their fields
differently. None of that holds any more. A guide that hands out a
command the app refuses is a bug whichever of the two is wrong.

Let's give edit the option format, drop the limitation box, replace
every example, and say that -t "" clears the tags where a bare t/ used
to. The notes about the command format no longer contrast the two
commands, since both now read the same way.

UserGuideExamplesTest checks that every add command printed in the guide
parses. Let's generalise it over a command word and a parser and run
edit's examples through it too, so the guide cannot drift from either
command again.

commitResults.messageTitle: Record edit's options in the Developer Guide
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide heads the section on option parsing "How add reads
its arguments" and closes it by recording edit's prefixes as a known
limitation to be fixed under issue #105. It also tells a reader that a
name holding a prefix fails to parse, that edit has no spelling for
clearing a field, and that edit recognizes prefixes after an ASCII
space. A reader following any of that would be misled about the code in
front of them.

Let's widen the section to both commands, replace the limitation with
why an explicitly empty value clears a field where a bare option cannot,
and correct the glossary and the Name and Email notes. The manual
testing appendix gains an "Editing a student" section covering the name
that AB3's prefixes made impossible to type, the clearing spelling and
its refusals, and the several-mistakes-at-once message, and its
follow-up cases now use the option that toggles the flag.

commitResults.messageTitle: Remove the unused prefix parsing classes
commitResults.messageBody:
Prefix, CliSyntax, ArgumentTokenizer and ArgumentMultimap read a
command's arguments as values each marked by a prefix such as p/. No
command is parsed that way once edit takes options, so the four classes
and their tests sit in the tree with no caller. Messages carries two
helpers for naming prefixes, getErrorMessageForDuplicatePrefixes and
getErrorMessageForMissingPrefixes, which are unreachable for the same
reason.

Let's delete all of them, along with the MessagesTest cases that exist
only to cover the two helpers. The flag equivalents the parsers call,
getErrorMessageForDuplicateFlags and getErrorMessageForMissingFields,
keep their own tests.

commitResults.messageTitle: Update the parser class diagram for the option classes
commitResults.messageBody:
The parser class diagram shows CliSyntax, ArgumentMultimap,
ArgumentTokenizer and Prefix, none of which exist any more. A developer
reading the Logic component against the code would be looking for four
classes that are not there, and would not find the five that replaced
them.

Let's show CliFlags, Flag, CommandTokenizer, FlagTokenizer and
FlagArgumentMap in their place, with FlagTokenizer depending on
CommandTokenizer so the two passes are visible. The surrounding text
gains a line naming those passes and pointing at the section that
explains why there are two.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep edit covered by the separator test
commitResults.messageBody:
parseCommand_everySeparator_givesTheSameCommandAsASpace checks that each
command reads the same way whichever whitespace character separates the
command word from its arguments, comparing against the ordinary space.
It spells its edit case with a prefix, which the option syntax no longer
accepts, so both sides of the comparison are now refused and the
assertion compares null with null. The test passes for all 25 whitespace
characters while checking nothing about edit.

Let's spell the case as edit 1 -p 91234567, and assert that the
space-separated baseline parses before comparing anything to it. The
assertion holds for every command in the list, so a later syntax change
that leaves one of them unparseable fails the test rather than quietly
emptying it. The comment above it no longer says add is alone in reading
its arguments with the tokenizer.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '105-take-edits-fields-as-options' into 105-remove-the-prefix-parsing-classes
Cap the length of an email a command may enter
commitResults.messageBody:
Email.isValidEmail matches VALIDATION_REGEX, whose local part nests one
quantifier inside another. Java matches a repeated group by recursion,
one frame per repetition, so an address with enough .-separated groups
exhausts the stack: "a." repeated 1500 times throws StackOverflowError
instead of returning false. That is an Error, and CommandBox catches
only CommandException and ParseException, so the command box keeps the
text, nothing turns red, and the User is told nothing at all.

Let's have ParserUtil.parseEmail clear Email.isWithinLengthLimit before
matching. The bound is 254 characters, the limit RFC 5321 section
4.5.3.1 puts on a forward path, so it comes from the domain rather than
from the parser and no real address meets it. It is also the only bound
measured to be safe on every stack size tried: on a 256 KB stack even a
513-character address overflows. getFailureReason carries the same
guard, since it matches the local part on its own.

isValidEmail keeps no length limit of its own. Storage validates with
it, and a narrower rule there would make a file an earlier version had
written unloadable; a failed load starts an empty book, so the next save
would discard records the product had already accepted.

A data file hand-edited to hold an address of several thousand
characters therefore still fails while loading. Reporting that belongs
with the unreadable-data handling in issue #144.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document the email length limit
commitResults.messageBody:
The User Guide gives no limit on the length of an email, and the
Developer Guide's note on the field says nothing about how the address
is validated. A limit the User can run into has to be written down,
with the reason it exists.

Let's say in the User Guide that an address may run to 254 characters
and that a longer one is refused with its length named. The Developer
Guide records why the bound exists, why it sits in the parser rather
than in the field, and that a data file holding a much longer address
still fails to load, which issue #144 covers. The manual testing
appendix gains the cases for the refusal and for an address at the
limit.

commitResults.messageTitle: Dress the window in the product's own theme
commitResults.messageBody:
docs/images/Ui.png shows TAB in a dark navy palette with rounded
surfaces. The window wears AB3's instead: mid-grey panes, a striped
list, a title reading "Address App", and a result box fixed at 100px
whatever it holds, so a one-line result leaves a gap and a longer one is
cut off. Anyone comparing the product against the picture it ships sees
two different applications.

Let's name the palette once at the top of DarkTheme.css and refer to the
names from every rule below it, so a shade is changed in one place
rather than hunted through the rules that use it. The window takes the
product's name, the list drops its striping because the mockup's rows
are uniform, a card and the command line become rounded surfaces, a tag
reads as a chip, and the row the User is on is marked by an accent down
its left edge rather than a border all the way round.

A TextArea paints its inside from -fx-control-inner-background, so the
result area kept showing the default white slab until that was set
rather than only -fx-background-color. It now wraps its text and sizes
to three rows, which is enough for a command that reports more than one
bad field at once.

ThemeTest guards the two things that fail silently: a stylesheet named
by MainWindow.fxml that does not resolve, and a colour written straight
into a rule rather than taken from the palette.

commitResults.messageTitle: Redesign the student card
commitResults.messageBody:
A card prints each field on its own line: the index and name, then the
tags, then the phone, then the email, then the follow-up marker. Five
rows for a record the mockup reads in two, and the index carries a
trailing dot the mockup does not draw.

Let's lay the card out as docs/images/Ui.png does. The index sits in
muted grey to the left, the name is bold with its tag chips beside it,
and the phone and email share one quieter line below. The follow-up
marker moves into a pill at the trailing edge of the name row, which is
where an age belongs once a follow-up records when it was raised.

The card also lays out a slot for the NUS ID. No student carries one
yet, so it is left out of the card the same way a missing email already
is, and the field can fill it without the UI being touched again. A card
must not show a detail the product does not hold, so nothing stands in
for it meanwhile.

The three label states the card can be in now share one helper rather
than repeating the unmanaged-and-invisible pair.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a summary sidebar beside the student list
commitResults.messageBody:
docs/images/Ui.png carries a sidebar: how many students are waiting on
a reply, which tags are in use and how many students carry each, and
the total at the foot. The window shows none of it, so a teaching
assistant has to run a command to learn what their cohort looks like.

Let's put a fixed-width summary panel to the left of the list. It
counts the list the window is showing rather than the whole student
book, so a search narrows the summary along with the list, and it
follows the list as commands change it. Tags are ordered by count and
alphabetically among ties, so that two equally used tags do not swap
places between runs. Nothing in the model, the storage or any command
changes: every number is derived from the students already on screen.

Narrowing the list uncovered a defect that predates the sidebar. A list
cell asked for the width its content wanted, so a long name or tag
pushed the list sideways behind a horizontal scroll bar instead of
being elided. A cell now asks for no width of its own and is laid out
to the width the list has, and the name keeps its natural width so the
spacer beside it cannot squeeze it into an ellipsis while the row still
has room to spare.

commitResults.messageTitle: Colour the command line as it is typed
commitResults.messageBody:
The command box is an undecorated text field. docs/images/Ui.png draws
a shell prompt instead: a marker, a monospace face, and the typed
command coloured so that the command word, its options and its quoted
values are told apart at a glance. For a CLI-first product that is the
most-used control in the window.

Let's give the line a prompt and paint the command behind it.
CommandHighlighter decides the colouring and knows nothing about
JavaFX, so the decision is checked on its own: it splits a command the
way the parser's own tokenizer does, quoting and escapes included, and
a quoted word is a value even when it opens with the option marker.

Nothing is ever rejected here. A command is coloured while it is still
half-typed, so an unclosed quote is ordinary and the parser keeps the
job of complaining when the command is submitted.

A TextField cannot colour its own content, so the colours are painted
on a TextFlow behind a field whose own text is transparent. The field
keeps the caret, the selection and every key pressed. The copy cannot
scroll with the field, so once a command outgrows the line the colours
are dropped and the field shows its own text again rather than sitting
misaligned beneath it.

The line also takes focus when the window opens. Every task is meant to
be reachable from the keyboard alone, and the caret belonged in the one
place the User types rather than somewhere they had to click first.

commitResults.messageTitle: SummaryPanelTest: Cover the panel, not only its arithmetic
commitResults.messageBody:
The tests reach only the static counting, so nothing exercises the
panel itself: the rows it builds, the numbers it writes into its
labels, or the listener that keeps them current. Codecov reported the
patch short of its threshold for exactly that reason, and the
behaviour a reader most wants pinned down, that the summary follows the
displayed list, went unchecked.

Let's build the panel on the toolkit the way StudentCardTest already
does and read the labels back: the counts for a mixed book, zeroes for
an empty one rather than a blank panel, and the summary following the
list when a command replaces what is on display.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '164-add-a-summary-sidebar' into 165-colour-the-command-line
Take the theme's colours and fonts from the mockup
commitResults.messageBody:
The palette was written by eye and three of its choices are wrong
against docs/images/Ui.png. The command line is drawn as a surface
raised above the window where the mockup sinks it into one, a card is
darker than the window where the mockup makes it lighter, and the
sidebar shares the window's colour instead of sitting below it. The
corners are rounder than the mockup draws them.

Every rule also names "Segoe UI", which exists only on Windows, so the
family resolves to whatever fontconfig picks elsewhere and "Segoe UI
Semibold" loses its weight altogether: a student's name is not bold on
Linux or macOS at all.

Let's read the colours out of the mockup instead of guessing them, name
each one after the thing it paints, and record beside it where it was
sampled. Families become stacks that resolve everywhere, and weight is
asked for with -fx-font-weight rather than by naming a Windows family.

The menu bar also kept AB3's 14pt label, which is half again the size
of anything else in the window.

The result area no longer holds a fixed three rows. It sizes to what it
has to say, and leaves the window when it has nothing, which is what
left the empty band under the command line before the first command.

Keep the selected card's rounded shape
commitResults.messageBody:
A one-sided border cannot follow a corner, so marking the selected row
with a border down its left edge squared that side of the card while
every other card stayed rounded.

Let's paint the accent as a rounded layer with the card surface laid
three points in from the left on top of it, which keeps one shape for
every row. The result line also loses its focus ring and its control
padding, so it reads as a line of text on the window rather than as a
box sitting in one.

Let a card label keep the colour it asks for
commitResults.messageBody:
A blanket rule paints every label inside a list cell in the ordinary
text colour. Two class selectors outrank the one a card label carries,
so a detail that asks to be muted is overruled and the whole card comes
out at one brightness.

Let's drop the blanket rule. Every label in a card names the class that
colours it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '162-dress-the-window-in-the-products-theme' into 163-redesign-the-student-card
Bold a student's name, as the mockup draws it
commitResults.messageBody:
The card's name rule names Segoe UI Semibold, a family that exists only
on Windows. Everywhere else it resolves to a regular face and the name
is no heavier than the detail beneath it. The card's other rules name
Segoe UI and monospace with the same problem.

Let's ask for the weight with -fx-font-weight and give each a family
stack that resolves wherever the app runs.

Line the prompt up with the command it introduces
commitResults.messageBody:
The prompt is set a size larger than the text beside it and the row
centres the two, so the marker sits slightly above the line it belongs
to.

Let's set it at the size of the command text and align the row on the
baseline, which is what lines up two runs of text rather than two
boxes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Stop the text field inheriting a bold face
commitResults.messageBody:
Swapping the Windows-only Semibold family for a stack plus a weight
left -fx-font-weight: bold on .text-field, so everything typed into the
command line came out bold.

Draw the prompt, the field and the colours in one font
commitResults.messageBody:
The field draws the placeholder and the caret while the flow behind it
draws what was typed, so the two have to be set identically or the
placeholder sits off the line. They were not: the field named the bare
family monospace and inherited a bold weight, the flow named a stack at
a normal one.

Aligning the row on the baseline made it worse rather than better. A
StackPane carries no text baseline, so the row stretched and pushed the
prompt above the line it introduces.

Let's pin the prompt, the field and the coloured runs to one family,
size and weight, and centre the row again.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give the prompt the same font stack as the line
commitResults.messageBody:
Two rules still name the bare family monospace, which resolves to
whatever fontconfig picks and need not be what the stack beside it
resolves to. The prompt is also still a size larger than the text it
introduces.

commitResults.messageTitle: Set the command's reply apart from the window
commitResults.messageBody:
The result reads as a stray line of grey text under the command line,
in the same colour and weight as a detail on a card, so nothing marks
it as the answer to what was just run.

Let's give it a surface of its own with an accent down its leading
edge, the same pairing that marks the selected row, and bring the text
back to the ordinary colour.

commitResults.messageTitle: Set the command's reply apart from the window
commitResults.messageBody:
The result reads as a stray line of grey text under the command line,
in the same colour and weight as a detail on a card, so nothing marks
it out as the answer to what was just run.

Let's give it a surface of its own with an accent down its leading
edge, the pairing that already marks the selected row, and bring the
text back to the ordinary colour.

Give the command line a caret of its own
commitResults.messageBody:
The field draws its caret in its text colour, and that colour is
transparent while the coloured copy is showing, so there is no cursor
at all once anything is typed.

Let's draw one. The line is monospace, so a character is the same width
wherever it falls and the caret sits at that width times the number of
characters before it, which avoids repeating the flow's own layout. It
blinks the way the field's own caret would have.

commitResults.messageTitle: Show a command's reply as a line, not a slab
commitResults.messageBody:
A text area reserves room for a fixed number of rows whatever it
holds, so a one-line reply sat in a box several times its height, and
giving that box a surface of its own only made the slab more obvious.
The mockup shows the reply as a line of text with a quiet rule beside
it.

Let's use a label, which is exactly as tall as what it has to say and
wraps rather than scrolling, so a command reporting several bad fields
hides none of them. The surface goes; a two point rule down the
leading edge is all that marks it out.

Measure the caret against the font beside it
commitResults.messageBody:
The caret is placed by counting the characters before it and
multiplying by the width of one. That assumes the field and the
coloured copy behind it resolved to the same font, and they need not,
so the caret drifts further from the text with every character typed.

Let's measure the run of text before the caret in the font the copy is
actually drawn in. It costs one Text per keystroke and holds for a
proportional face as well as a monospace one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Paint the window behind the panes
commitResults.messageBody:
Each pane paints its own background and nothing paints the window
behind them, so the scene's default white shows through anywhere a
pane does not. Turning the result strip into a line with only a rule
on it left exactly such a gap, and a white band appeared under the
command line.

Let's give the root its own colour so no future pane can expose the
scene again.

Measure each run of the command in its own font
commitResults.messageBody:
The caret is placed by measuring the text before it in the font of the
first run. That run is the command word, which is drawn bold and so is
wider than everything after it, and the caret ends up past the end of
the line by roughly the extra width of that one word.

Let's walk the runs and measure each in the font it is drawn in.

commitResults.messageTitle: Mark the reply with the accent, not a border grey
commitResults.messageBody:
The rule beside the command's reply is drawn in the colour used for a
divider, which is near enough to the window to disappear, so the reply
still reads as a stray line rather than as an answer.

Let's draw it in the accent, which is the colour already marking the
selected row, and keep it to two points so it stays a rule.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '162-dress-the-window-in-the-products-theme' into 163-redesign-the-student-card

Line the prompt glyph up with the text
commitResults.messageBody:
The row centres the prompt and the command line as boxes, but the
ornament sits low within its own em box, so what is drawn comes out
about a point below the lowercase beside it.

Let's lift it by that point.

commitResults.messageTitle: Cover a backslash typed as the last character
commitResults.messageBody:
A backslash at the very end of a command has nothing to escape, and
the branch that checks for that was the one line of the highlighter no
test reached.

Let's type one, and assert it is neither swallowed nor allowed to send
the scan past the end of the command.

commitResults.messageTitle: Hand the line back to the field whenever the colours do not fit
commitResults.messageBody:
Three faults in the fallback, all from deciding once, on a change of
text, and only hiding the copy.

The line narrowing is not a change of text, so a command typed in a
wide window stayed coloured when the window shrank, with the copy
wrapping while the field it sits behind did not. The width is watched
now.

Hiding the copy left it managed, and a TextFlow wraps, so a long
command kept asking for the height of every wrapped line and the
command box grew with it. It is unmanaged now as well as hidden.

The caret stayed on whenever the field had focus. Once the field shows
its own text it draws its own caret, so ours was a second one, placed
without regard to the field's scrolling. It goes with the colours.

The command line also asked for fonts that need not be installed, and
JavaFX answers an unknown family with System rather than trying the
next one, so the line was set in a proportional face. Monospaced is a
logical family and maps to a real monospace font everywhere, and the
size matches the mockup at 15px.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep a long reply reachable
commitResults.messageBody:
A label is exactly as tall as its text, which fixed the band of empty
space, but it cannot scroll and cannot be selected. A reply too long
for the room then has no way of being read: at a narrow window a
command reporting four bad fields loses the last of them.

Let's go back to a text area and take its height from the text once it
has been laid out, rather than from a whole number of rows. The area is
then as tall as its content wrapped at the width it actually has, stops
growing at 120 points, and scrolls past that, so nothing it has to say
is out of reach.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep the follow-up pill inside the card
commitResults.messageBody:
The name is pinned to its natural width so that a spacer could not
squeeze it, which means it never yields. A realistic long name with a
long tag beside it therefore makes the row wider than the card, and
what sits at the trailing edge goes over the side: the follow-up pill
ends up outside the list altogether.

Let's protect the pill instead. It keeps its natural width, the name
yields once the row has genuinely run out of room and is elided rather
than pushing anything out, and the tags and the spacer may shrink to
nothing.

The NUS ID also asked for fonts that need not be installed, and JavaFX
answers an unknown family with System rather than trying the next one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '163-redesign-the-student-card' into 164-add-a-summary-sidebar
Spell out what may shrink in a card row
commitResults.messageBody:
The row's widths were left to work themselves out, so whether the
follow-up pill stayed in the card depended on which element happened to
give way first.

Let's say it: the pill keeps its natural width, the name may shrink to
forty points before it is elided, and the tags and the spacer may give
up everything.

commitResults.messageTitle: Let the tag list scroll inside the sidebar
commitResults.messageBody:
A cohort can carry more tags than the window is tall. The sidebar grew
to fit all of them, so the later tags, the student total and the foot
of the panel all ended up below the bottom of the window with no way to
reach them.

Let's put the tag list in a scroll pane that takes whatever height is
left, so the total stays at the foot of the sidebar and the tags scroll
within the room above it. The pane is styled to disappear into the
sidebar rather than read as a control.

commitResults.messageTitle: Remove conflict markers left in the stylesheet
commitResults.messageBody:
A merge of the theme branch was committed with its conflict unresolved,
so DarkTheme.css carries <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> lines. JavaFX
reports a parse error for them and carries on, dropping the rules
around them without saying which, so the card styling and the result
area silently stopped applying.

Both sides of that conflict only added rules, and the closing brace
after the marker belonged to each of them, so let's keep both blocks
and give each its own. The rule eliding a value too long for its row
was lost with the markers and comes back too.

commitResults.messageTitle: Remove conflict markers left in the stylesheet
commitResults.messageBody:
The same unresolved merge reached this branch. Both sides of it only
added rules, so let's keep each and give each its own closing brace,
and bring back the rule eliding a value too long for its row.

commitResults.messageTitle: Stop the tag pane claiming four hundred points
commitResults.messageBody:
A FlowPane's prefWrapLength defaults to 400, and a horizontal FlowPane
reports that as its preferred width whatever it holds. The tag pane
therefore asked for 400 points for a single chip, the row's preferred
width came to more than the card had, and the HBox shrank what it
could: the name went to its minimum and was elided even with most of
the row standing empty. Resizing the list made it worse, since the
elided width stuck.

Let's set the wrap length to one, so the pane asks for what its chips
actually need. It still wraps at whatever width it is given.

commitResults.messageTitle: Bound a card to the list rather than starving it
commitResults.messageBody:
Asking the cell for no width at all does stop a long name pushing the
list sideways, but it leaves the card laying itself out in no room, so
every name is elided to its minimum and stays that way once the list
has been resized.

Let's hold the card to the list's width instead. Each part of the card
keeps its preferred width until the card really has run out of room.

The layout tests also built their scenes without the stylesheet, so
they were measuring text in the default font rather than the one the
product shows. They share a helper that dresses the scene now.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '164-add-a-summary-sidebar' into 165-colour-the-command-line
Resolve the merge left unresolved in the card and the stylesheet
commitResults.messageBody:
A merge of the card branch was committed with its conflicts in place,
so StudentListCard.fxml and DarkTheme.css both carry <<<<<<<, =======
and >>>>>>> lines. The card then fails to load at all, and JavaFX
reports a parse error for the stylesheet and carries on without the
rules around the markers.

Let's keep the sidebar rules this branch adds, take the card rules from
the branch it merges, and leave one rule for eliding a value too long
for its row rather than the two the conflict left. The sidebar's fonts
also still named families that exist only on Windows.

commitResults.messageTitle: Resolve the merge left unresolved on this branch too
commitResults.messageBody:
The same merge reached this branch with its conflicts in place, so the
card would not load and the stylesheet lost the rules around its
markers.

Let's take the card and the stylesheet from the branch this one
follows, and put back only the command line rules, which exist nowhere
else.

The caret is also no longer placed from the text listener. JavaFX
reports a new caret position before it reports the new text, so that
listener measured the caret against the copy of the previous command
and the User saw it jump there and back on every keystroke. The
recolour that follows places it against a copy that matches.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep a card's tags on one line
commitResults.messageBody:
A FlowPane reports its prefWrapLength as its preferred width whatever
it holds. The default is 400, so the pane asked for 400 points for a
single chip and the name beside it was squeezed to its minimum and
elided with most of the row standing empty. Setting a small wrap length
fixed the name and then stacked two chips one above the other instead.

Let's use a row. It asks for what its chips need, and keeps them on the
line the mockup draws them on.

commitResults.messageTitle: Take the command line's colours from the mockup
commitResults.messageBody:
The option colour was guessed. docs/images/Ui.png draws an option in a
muted mauve and the value after it in a light grey blue, where the
palette had the option in the same blue family as the command word and
the value in ordinary white. Sampled across -i, -e, -t and
--follow-up, the mockup is consistent.

Let's name both shades after what they paint.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '162-dress-the-window-in-the-products-theme' into 163-redesign-the-student-card
Merge branch '163-redesign-the-student-card' into 164-add-a-summary-sidebar

Colour a plain value as the mockup does
commitResults.messageBody:
A value given to an option is drawn in ordinary text colour, where the
mockup draws it a shade dimmer than the window's brightest text so
that the command word and the quoted values stand out against it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Measure a span in the font it will be drawn in
commitResults.messageBody:
A Text added to the coloured copy has not had the stylesheet applied
when the caret is placed, so asking it for its font gives the default
proportional one. The caret is positioned from those fonts, so on a
monospace line it advanced by a proportional amount and came to rest
partway through a character: typing list left it between the i and
the s.

Let's apply the stylesheet to the copy as soon as it is rebuilt, before
anything measures it. The advances are then even, which is what the new
test asserts.

The command box tests also built their scenes without the stylesheet,
so they could not have caught this. They share the helper that dresses
a scene now.

commitResults.messageTitle: Take the caret's height and place from the text beside it
commitResults.messageBody:
A bar of a fixed height centred in the line does not sit where the
text does: a font's ink is not centred in its line box, so the caret
came out about a point below the characters it stands between.

Let's give it the height of a run of the text and line it up with that
run's own centre, which holds whatever font or size the line is set
in.

commitResults.messageTitle: Scroll the colours instead of switching them off
commitResults.messageBody:
A command longer than the line gave up its colours and handed the text
back to the field. The colouring is the point of the line, so losing
it exactly when a command gets interesting is the wrong trade.

Let's scroll the copy with the command. The field keeps its caret in
view by scrolling, and this follows the same rule, so the two stay
together without the field having to report an offset it does not
expose.

Two things made that possible. The copy and the caret now sit in a
plain Pane, which neither resizes what it holds nor grows with it: a
StackPane does both, so the copy of a long command dragged the command
box wider than the window. The Pane is clipped, so the copy runs off
the edge the way the field's own text does, and a TextFlow sized to
its content stays on one line rather than wrapping and making the box
taller.

Clearing a long command also left the caret at the height that command
had needed. An empty line takes the height of one line of the field's
own font.

commitResults.messageTitle: Draw the selection, and let the field show nothing itself
commitResults.messageBody:
Two layers were visible at once. The field drew its own text in white
over the coloured copy, because the rule hiding it keyed off a state
that went away with the fallback, and it drew its own selection
highlight at the offset it had scrolled to rather than the offset the
copy is drawn at, so the highlight broke into fragments between the
characters.

Let's have the field show neither. It keeps the input, the caret
position and the selection; the line draws the text, the caret and now
the selected run, all measured the same way.

commitResults.messageTitle: Size the selection band by preference, not by resizing it
commitResults.messageBody:
A managed child is laid out at its preferred size, so resizing the
band had no effect and it stayed nothing by nothing: selecting a
command showed no selection at all.

commitResults.messageTitle: Let only the name give way in a card row
commitResults.messageBody:
A long name squeezed everything beside it: the tag chip came down to
an ellipsis, which says nothing at all, and the follow-up pill was
only just holding its place.

Let's take the pill out of the row that gives way, so a name can never
push it out of the card whatever its length, and let the tags keep
their width. The name is the one part that yields, and it is elided.

Give the reply a row per line
commitResults.messageBody:
Taking the height from the laid-out text read the wrong node and
returned the height of the whole viewport, so a one line reply sat in
a box several times its height.

Let's count the lines instead: a row each, up to six, and scroll past
that. The area still disappears when there is nothing to report, and
is still a text area, so a reply too long to show at once can be
scrolled to and selected.

Bound both sides of a card's first row
commitResults.messageBody:
Letting only the name give way fixed a long name and broke a long tag:
one enormous tag took the whole row, crushed the name to a few letters
and ran under the follow-up pill. Letting only the tags give way did
the reverse.

Let's bound both. The name keeps a readable stretch, each chip is
capped so one long tag cannot take the row, and the tags keep enough
width for the start of a chip to be read, but only when there are tags
to show.
