Bound a card to the list rather than starving it
commitResults.messageBody:
Asking the cell for no width at all stops a long name pushing the list
sideways, but it leaves the card laying itself out in no room, so every
name is elided to its minimum and stays that way once the list has been
resized.

Let's hold the card to the list's width instead. Each part of the card
keeps its preferred width until the card really has run out of room.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '164-add-a-summary-sidebar' into 165-colour-the-command-line
Align a card's tags against the pill
commitResults.messageBody:
Each card's tags started wherever that card's name happened to end, so
a list of long names read as a ragged edge.

Let's give the name whatever the row has left. It then elides at much
the same place on every card, and the tags line up against the pill at
the trailing edge.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '164-add-a-summary-sidebar' into 165-colour-the-command-line
Merge branch '163-redesign-the-student-card' into 164-add-a-summary-sidebar
Mark a refused command on the copy, not on the field
commitResults.messageBody:
Extensions.css marks a refusal with an important text fill, which beat
the rule keeping the field's own text out of sight, so the field
painted its text in red over the coloured copy at its own scroll
offset: two overlapping sets of characters.

Let's keep the field transparent whatever else asks otherwise, and
mark the refusal on the copy, which is the text the User is reading.

commitResults.messageTitle: Show a card's name and tags at a readable length
commitResults.messageBody:
A card is a summary, and one enormous value crowded out the rest of
the record: a long name squeezed the chips beside it down to single
letters, and five chips on one row came out as five ellipses. Eliding
on width alone cannot prevent that, because what is left depends on
what else happens to be in the row.

Let's cut by characters instead, which is the same on every card: the
name at 42, a chip at 16, and at most three chips before the rest are
counted. The whole of anything cut is a hover away, so a card
summarises the record without putting any of it out of reach.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '163-redesign-the-student-card' into 164-add-a-summary-sidebar
Merge branch '164-add-a-summary-sidebar' into 165-colour-the-command-line
Set a card's tags beside the name
commitResults.messageBody:
A card's tags are right-aligned against the follow-up pill, so they
start wherever the row has space left rather than against the name they
describe. The pill is also left out of a card whose student is not
flagged, which hands that card's tags the space the pill would have
taken: the chips then sit further right than the chips on a flagged
card, and a reader going down the list sees them jump between two
columns.

Let's keep the name at its own width and set the tags immediately after
it, leaving the chips in the same place whatever else the card holds,
and keep the pill at the card's trailing edge.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '163-redesign-the-student-card' into 164-add-a-summary-sidebar
Merge branch '164-add-a-summary-sidebar' into 165-colour-the-command-line
Cut a card's name and tags to a fixed size
commitResults.messageBody:
A card shares one row between the name, the tags and the follow-up
pill, and the row shares out what it cannot fit among all three. A
student with many tags asks for a row many chips wide, which leaves the
name beside it almost nothing: the name comes out as an ellipsis, and
every chip is cut to two or three letters that name no tag. A name is
also cut wherever the row happens to run out, so the same name breaks
off at a different place from one card to the next.

Let's cut a name at a fixed count of characters and hold it at that
width, and let the tags give way instead: a row of chips shows the
first three tags it has room for whole and counts the rest in a
trailing chip, which names them on hover. The whole of anything cut is
a hover away, and a card too narrow for its name keeps the pill at its
edge rather than painting over it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '163-redesign-the-student-card' into 164-add-a-summary-sidebar
Merge branch '164-add-a-summary-sidebar' into 165-colour-the-command-line
Compare a card's name against the width it asked for
commitResults.messageBody:
The test that holds a long name to one cut compares the width the row
gave the name against the width it asked for, and allows half a pixel
between them. A row rounds a width to whole pixels, so the two can sit
a whole pixel apart, and whether they do depends on the font the
machine has: the test passes here and fails on the Linux runner.

Let's allow a pixel between them, and say both numbers when it fails,
so that a failure names the width the name was cut to.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '163-redesign-the-student-card' into 164-add-a-summary-sidebar
Merge branch '164-add-a-summary-sidebar' into 165-colour-the-command-line
Email validation overflows the stack on a very long address #160 (#161)
Give way in one order on a card's first line
commitResults.messageBody:
A card's first line shares what it cannot fit between the name and the
tags beside it, so both lose about half of what they asked for. On a
narrow card the tags disappear while the name holds its full length,
and the name is then cut off against the edge of the card with no
ellipsis to say that it was.

Let's give way in one order instead. The name keeps the length the card
cuts it to while the line has room for it, so the same name breaks off
at the same place from one card to the next. Below that the name gives
way and is cut again with an ellipsis, down to the point where it would
crowd out the tags: a card that has tags shows the start of one however
narrow it is.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '164-add-a-summary-sidebar' into 165-colour-the-command-line
Merge branch '163-redesign-the-student-card' into 164-add-a-summary-sidebar
Check a card with no tags leaves no gap
commitResults.messageBody:
The line that gives way in one order between a card's name and its
tags decides what a card with no tags at all looks like, and no test
covers that card: a row that reserved space for chips it does not have
would leave a gap the name could have used, and nothing would say so.

Let's check that such a card gives the whole line to the name.

Scroll the command line only when the caret leaves it
commitResults.messageBody:
The coloured copy of the command works out where to draw the line from
on every change, from the caret alone, which puts the caret near the
right-hand edge whatever it was doing before. A field scrolls only when
the caret would leave the part of the command it is showing, and stays
where it is otherwise. So on a command longer than the line, moving the
caret left drags the copy back under the caret while the field stays
put: the copy then shows a different part of the command from the one
the field hit-tests a click against, and a click lands on the wrong
character.

Let's keep where the line is drawn from between one change and the
next, and move it only far enough to bring the caret back into view.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test what happens when a command is entered
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing covers what the command line does with the command it is
given: that it runs it and clears the line, that Enter on an empty
line is not a command, that a command the parser refuses stays on the
line and is marked, and that the mark comes off as soon as it is being
corrected. The four listeners that put the colours back where they
belong are written out four times, and the one for focus is never
reached by a test.

Let's cover each of those, and name the listener once so that all four
ask for the same thing by name.

commitResults.messageTitle: Draw a card's name no wider than its own text
commitResults.messageBody:
The line that holds a card's name and its tags gives the name whatever
room the tags leave, and the name draws its text at the left of it. The
tags therefore start where the name's box ends rather than where its
text does, which puts them out at the right of the line and leaves a
gap that grows as the name gets shorter.

Let's draw the name no wider than its text needs. The test that holds
the chips against the name measures where the name's box ends, which is
why it passed, so let's measure where its text ends instead.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '164-add-a-summary-sidebar' into 165-colour-the-command-line
Merge branch '163-redesign-the-student-card' into 164-add-a-summary-sidebar
Draw the command line where the field draws it
commitResults.messageBody:
Three things on the command line disagree with what is behind them. The
lane is clipped to the size it has when its width arrives, and a region
is given its width before its height, so the clip is as tall as nothing
and the line comes up blank however much is typed into it. The copy
keeps a margin beyond the caret that the field does not, so a click
lands a character or two from the one it was aimed at. The colouring
asks Character.isWhitespace where the parser asks for the pattern that
also covers the non-breaking space a pasted command carries, and treats
a backslash as escaping whatever follows where the parser escapes only
a quote or another backslash, so a command is coloured as something
other than what running it does.

Let's follow both sides of the lane with the clip, bring the caret back
no further than its edge, and ask the tokenizer itself where a token
ends.

commitResults.messageTitle: Mark the selected run of a command visibly
commitResults.messageBody:
The band behind the selected run of a command is drawn in the colour
that marks the row the User is on, which is a shade away from the line
behind it. Against that line it reads as nothing: selecting the whole
command with Ctrl+A looks no different from selecting none of it, so
there is no way to see what a copy or an overtype is about to take.

Let's draw the band in the line's own accent, carried at the strength
that tells it apart from the line while leaving the command on top of
it legible.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give a wrapped reply the rows it needs
commitResults.messageBody:
The reply area takes a row for each line the reply was written with.
A reply is wrapped at the width of the area as well, and the common
ones arrive on a single line: "Edited student: ..." carries the name,
the phone, the email and the tags on one line, so the area takes one
row and everything past the first row is hidden. On a narrow window
that is most of the reply.

Let's count the rows the reply takes once it is wrapped at the width
the area has, and count them again when that width changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Write the window in a font the machine has
commitResults.messageBody:
The stylesheet names a list of families for each piece of text, the
way a web page does. JavaFX reads only the first of them: where that
family is missing it falls back to the system font and never tries the
next, so a machine carrying one of the others is written in neither.

Let's choose the family against the families the machine reports, and
set it on the window for everything in it to inherit, leaving a rule
to name a family only where it wants a different one.

Hold a card to the width of the list
commitResults.messageBody:
A card lays itself out at whatever width its content asks for, and the
list puts a horizontal scroll bar under it rather than holding it back.
On a narrow window the list is then scrolled sideways, and the pill at
a card's trailing edge sits off the side of it where it cannot be read
at all. The card is what outgrows the list, so the card is where this
belongs, rather than arriving with the sidebar that first made the list
narrow enough to notice.

Let's hold each card to the width the list has, and check it at a width
narrow enough that a card of its own size would outgrow it: at a
comfortable width the card fits either way, so the check passed with
the binding taken out and guarded nothing.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document the summary beside the list
commitResults.messageBody:
The sidebar is a feature a User sees every time they open the window,
and neither guide mentions it: a reader has no way to learn that the
counts follow the list rather than the whole book, which is the one
thing about it that can surprise. Its tag list also breaks a tie by
natural order, so a reader meets "Zoo" above "apple".

Let's say in the User Guide what the panel counts and that `find`
narrows it, say in the Developer Guide where the counts come from and
why, add a manual test for it, and break a tie without regard to case.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '164-add-a-summary-sidebar' into 165-colour-the-command-line
Catch the colours the theme test lets through
commitResults.messageBody:
The test that keeps colours in the palette looks only at properties
whose name holds "color", so -fx-text-fill and -fx-effect may carry
whatever they like, and it knows a colour only as a hex code or as the
word white. It also checks that six palette names exist rather than
that every name a rule refers to does, so a misspelt name goes through
and JavaFX drops the rule without a word. It says nothing about the
same selector being written twice, which leaves which colour wins to
the order of the file.

Let's look at every property, know a colour by name and by function as
well as by hex, check every name a rule uses against the palette, and
check each selector is written once. That finds a shadow drawn in
black and three selectors written twice, so let's name the shadow and
fold each pair into one rule. The window's smallest size is checked
against what it holds, so that it cannot be made too small to show it.

commitResults.messageBody:
The window may be dragged down to 450 wide. The sidebar beside the
list takes the width its content needs whatever the window does, so
below 490 the list is squeezed past its own minimum and what is in it
is cut off at the edge of the window.

Let's hold the window at the 490 its content needs.

commitResults.messageTitle: Cut a name where a reader would cut it
commitResults.messageBody:
A name or a tag longer than a card shows is cut at an index into the
string. An emoji is two characters as Java stores it, and a letter and
the accent that belongs to it are two more, so the cut can land in the
middle of one and leave half a character behind, which is drawn as a
broken glyph. Working out how many chips fit also writes on the chip
that counts the rest while it is still deciding what that chip should
say.

Let's cut where a reader would, between one character and the next,
and put the counting chip back as it was once it has been measured.

Mark a name as cut only when it was cut
commitResults.messageBody:
A name is cut to a number of characters as a reader counts them, but
whether it was cut at all is decided by the number Java stores it in.
An emoji is two of those and one of these, so a name of a few words and
a dozen emoji is under the limit as it reads and over it as it is
stored: the whole name is shown with an ellipsis after it, saying
something was taken off when nothing was, and carrying a tooltip that
repeats what is already on the card.

Let's cut first and mark it only when the cut took something off.

Merge branch '163-redesign-the-student-card' into 164-add-a-summary-sidebar
Keep the caret inside the line it is on
commitResults.messageBody:
The line scrolls only as far as the end of the command, which puts the
caret, standing after the last character, exactly on the edge where the
lane is clipped: at the end of a command long enough to scroll, the
caret is cut away and the User has nothing to type against. The test
written with it checks for that same position, so it passes.

Let's bring the caret itself back into the line rather than the point
it stands at, and let the line scroll the caret's width further than
the command alone needs.

commitResults.messageTitle: Measure a reply's rows against its own line
commitResults.messageBody:
How many rows a reply takes is worked out by dividing the height it
wraps to by the height of the letter X. The two are different glyphs:
in Inter a line of a reply stands 15.0 against the 14.52 of an X, so
the division comes to 1.03 and is rounded up. Every one-line reply
therefore takes two rows, and "Listed all students." carries an empty
row under it. The tests run in the system font, where the two happen
to agree.

Let's measure a row against a row of the same reply, taken before it
is wrapped, and check the replies a User sees most in each of the
fonts the window may be written in.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '162-dress-the-window-in-the-products-theme' into 163-redesign-the-student-card
Show a tag where the row has space for nothing else
commitResults.messageBody:
A row too narrow for one chip beside a count of the others shows only
the count: a card with two tags on a 450-wide window reads "2 more…",
which names neither of them, and contradicts what the row says it
does. The User Guide also describes the follow-up marker as a line of
its own on the card, which it has not been since the card was laid out
with the marker at its trailing edge.

Let's give such a row to the first tag, cut to what space there is,
since which tag a student carries says more than how many they have,
and describe the marker where it is.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '163-redesign-the-student-card' into 164-add-a-summary-sidebar
Keep a tag's count beside the tag however long it is
commitResults.messageBody:
A row in the summary shares what it cannot fit between the tag and its
count, so a long enough tag leaves the count reading as an ellipsis,
and the count is the one part of the row a reader cannot work out for
themselves. The cut tag carries no tooltip either, so neither half of
the row can be read. The UI diagram leaves the panel out, the Developer
Guide weighs up an alternative reading as though in a review comment,
and its manual test runs `find Siti` against sample data that holds no
Siti.

Let's cut the tag rather than its count, name the whole of it on
hover, put the panel in the diagram, state the decision rather than
debating it, and run the manual test against a student who is there.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '164-add-a-summary-sidebar' into 165-colour-the-command-line
Keep a selected command legible, and document it
commitResults.messageBody:
An option on the command line is drawn in a mauve that reads well
against the line but only just stands out from the band behind a
selection, so selecting a command takes half of it away. Neither guide
mentions the command line at all, and three comments in CommandBox
describe behaviour it no longer has: the colours are said to be
dropped once a command outgrows the line, which has not been true
since the copy learnt to scroll.

Let's lift the mauve until it reads on the band as well as on the
line, check every colour the line uses against that band rather than
the band alone, say in both guides what the line does, and describe
what the code does now.

commitResults.messageTitle: Dress the rest of the window in the same theme
commitResults.messageBody:
Two stylesheets are left as AddressBook wrote them. Extensions.css
marks a refused command in its own red, paints an empty row in its own
grey, and carries two rules for parts the product does not have.
HelpWindow.css dresses the help window in white on grey, so opening
help from a dark window opens a pale one. The test that keeps colours
in the palette reads only the main stylesheet, so neither was noticed.

Let's take the colours in both from the palette, which a looked-up
colour resolves against the node rather than the file it was written
in, drop the rules for parts that are not there, and read every
stylesheet the window loads rather than one of them.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '162-dress-the-window-in-the-products-theme' into 163-redesign-the-student-card
Find a card's first line by what is in it
commitResults.messageBody:
The first line of a card picks the name and the tags out of its
children by the order they were written in the layout file, so
swapping the two round there would draw each in the other's place and
look merely odd rather than wrong. How a chip is cut is also checked
twice, once through the row that cuts it and once through a card.

Let's pick each out by what it is, say so if one is missing, and leave
the chip to the test of the row that cuts it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Check the font chosen on a machine with none of ours
commitResults.messageBody:
Which family the window is written in is decided against the families
the machine reports, and the branch for a machine carrying none of the
preferred ones is never taken here, so nothing says what such a
machine gets.

Let's take the two lists as arguments so both answers can be asked
for, and check that a machine with none of them keeps its own family
and that the order preferred decides rather than the order installed.

Draw a card's chips and phone inside the card
commitResults.messageBody:
A row with space for one chip but not for a count beside it keeps the
chip and places the count after it anyway, half outside the row, where
it reads as "1 m". The second line of a card shares what it cannot fit
between the phone and the email, so a flagged student on a narrow
window shows a phone of "9111…", and half a phone number is of no use
to anyone where the start of an email still says whose it is.

The tests around both check little: the one for the pill uses a
student who has none, and the one for a long name asks only that the
card report some width at all.

Let's leave the count out when there is no room for it, keep the phone
whole and let the email give way, and check what is drawn rather than
what was asked for.

commitResults.messageTitle: Ask the reply area where it wraps
commitResults.messageBody:
How many rows a reply takes is worked out against a guess at the
area's width: its own width less twenty-six pixels for padding and a
scroll bar. The guess puts the wrap a few pixels from where the area
puts it, so a reply whose last word lands within those few pixels of
the edge is given a row it does not use. The count is also redone only
when the area's width changes, so widening the window after a long
reply leaves the area as tall as the reply used to be.

The help window has the same shape of problem: a stage is sized to its
scene when the layout file is read, before the address is put on the
label and before the theme has dressed the button, and that window
cannot be resized, so it showed "…/UserGuide.ht…" and "Copy U…".

Let's ask the area's own text node where it wraps and follow what it
draws, and size the help window to its content once it has been
dressed. The tests check the rows against what is drawn rather than
against a font's numbers, across sixty widths, so that neither guess
can come back unnoticed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Let the list give way before the reply does
commitResults.messageBody:
The panes of the window together ask for more height than a window
opened at its default 600 has, and a VBox short of room shrinks every
child whatever its grow priority. The reply is the one that suffers:
a five-line reply is squeezed into the room for four and the rest is
cut off, while the list beside it, which scrolls whatever it cannot
show, keeps its full height.

Let's hold the reply at the height it asks for and let the list give
way instead.

panel cuts it to, and not when the panel's own width cuts it: a tag of
eighteen characters or fewer reads as "CS2103T-TUTORI…" with nothing
to say what it was. The check that the count stays whole passes with
the rule that keeps it whole taken out, because it reads the count's
text rather than what is drawn.

it, and say in the check that the count is the part that may not be
squeezed.

Keep a refused command legible when selected
commitResults.messageBody:
A refused command is written in one red, and against the band behind
a selection that red stands at 2.12 to 1, so selecting the command to
correct it takes it away. Two claims in the guides also say more than
the code does: that the colouring asks the tokenizer where a token
ends, where it walks the command itself and asks the tokenizer only
the two questions the pair must agree on, and that ThemeTest checks
the contrast, where CommandBoxTest does.

Let's lift the red and lighten the band a little until every colour
the line uses stands clear of it, check the refused command as well as
the typed one, and say what the code does.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say what the code does now, and say it once
commitResults.messageBody:
Four comments describe code that has moved on: the clip on a card's
details is explained by a name that is no longer cut the way it says,
the copy of a command is explained against a StackPane it no longer
sits in, and the first line of a card is described as holding a name
that never gives way. Two constants name the same measurement, and
three tests reach for a class by its full name rather than importing
it. The parameter carrying how far the line has scrolled is also named
after the field it was read from.

Let's say what each does now, take the measurement from one place,
import what the tests use, and name the parameter for what it carries.

commitResults.messageTitle: Size the help window to the frame around it
commitResults.messageBody:
The help window is sized to its scene, and the scene was measured when
the layout file was read: before the address was put on its label and
before the theme dressed its button. The window cannot be resized, so
it showed "…/UserGuide.ht…" and "Copy U…". Sizing it to its scene
again does not help, because the scene is the thing that is too small.

Let's measure what the window draws and give the window that much,
plus whatever of it is frame rather than scene, once there is a frame
to measure.

Open the help window at a size that fits it

A scene is measured when its layout file is read, which for the help
window is before the address is put on its label and before the theme
has dressed its button, so the window opened too small for either and,
being pinned shut, stayed that way: it read "…/UserGuide.ht…" and
"Copy U…". Sizing it to its scene afterwards does not help, because
the scene is the thing that is too small.

Let's give the scene the size this window needs, hold the address and
the button to their own widths, and let the window be resized.

Count the reply's rows outside the layout pass
commitResults.messageBody:
The rows a reply takes are counted while the area is being laid out,
because that is when it has just wrapped the reply and can say where.
Changing the rows there changes how tall the area wants to be, and the
panes around it have already been laid out by then, so the area stays
at the height it had: the first reply after launch comes up several
rows too tall and stays that way, and widening the window leaves a
reply that no longer wraps as tall as it was.

The tests laid the scene out a second time "as a pulse would", which
the running window never does, so they saw none of it.

Let's ask again on the next pulse, when the window can lay out around
the answer, and let the tests run on pulses rather than on a pass of
their own.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '162-dress-the-window-in-the-products-theme' into 163-redesign-the-student-card
Say how many tags a narrow card left out

A row with space for one whole chip but not for a chip and a count
drops the count, which happens on cards up to about 526 wide: at 450
a card reads "AY2627 Sem 1…" with nothing to say that three more tags
exist. A lone chip is also stretched to fill the row, so one short tag
is drawn as a pill across the card.

Let's cut the chip and keep the count beside it, down to the width
where what is left of the chip would be an ellipsis and little else,
and draw a chip no wider than its own text. The sweep over widths
checks that a card showing some of a student's tags always says there
are more.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say what the card's code does, on the card's branch
commitResults.messageBody:
The comments on the card and its first line describe behaviour they no
longer have, the measurement kept in two constants is one measurement,
and a test reaches for a class by its full name. All of it was put
right on the branch that colours the command line, which owns none of
these files, so this branch and the two above it still carry the old
wording and would keep it if they merge first.

Let's make the change where the files live.

commitResults.messageTitle: Import what the reply test uses

tests, so this branch would keep the old spelling if it merges first.

Tie the panel to the tooltip it relies on

Two checks pass with the thing they check taken out: the panel's rows
are checked only against a tag longer than the count of characters it
is cut to, which the plainer helper also names on hover, and nothing
widens a label back to see the tooltip go again. The sidebar's own

may not shrink past is set without saying where it comes from.

back, make the documentation corrections where the sidebar lives, and
say what the 490 is.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say what the colour checks do and do not cover
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide says the colouring and the parser cannot drift
apart, where the check between them compares only how many tokens
each found, and it says the colours are checked for contrast without
saying against what bar. The bar is 3:1, which is what WCAG asks of
large text rather than of text this size, because a band light enough
to be seen against a window this dark leaves no room for 4.5:1
without moving every colour towards white.

Let's say what the check covers and what the bar is, so that the next
reader can weigh it rather than take it on trust.

commitResults.messageTitle: Give the help window a floor to rest on
commitResults.messageBody:
The help window may now be resized, which it needed to be, but nothing
stops it being dragged narrower than the address it exists to carry.
The comment explaining its sizing also still says it cannot be
resized.

Let's hold it at the size its content needs, and say what the sizing
is for now that the layout file gives the scene a size of its own.

Check what a narrow card promises, not its font
commitResults.messageBody:
The check on a card too narrow for a chip and a count pins the number
of chips to one, which depends on how wide the machine's font draws
them: it holds here and fails on the macOS runner, where one more
fits.

Let's check what the card promises at any width, which is that it
names a tag before it counts any.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '164-add-a-summary-sidebar' into 165-colour-the-command-line
Merge branch '163-redesign-the-student-card' into 164-add-a-summary-sidebar
Draw the copy where the field scrolled, caret apart
commitResults.messageBody:
The caret stands after the last character, so at the end of a command
long enough to scroll it falls on the edge of the line, where the lane
is clipped and nothing of it shows. Making room by scrolling the copy
a caret's width further moves the copy out of step with the field's
own text, and the field is what decides which character a click lands
on, so a click near the end of a long command lands a character out.

Let's keep the copy exactly where the field has scrolled to, and bring
the caret alone back inside the line.

commitResults.messageTitle: Show a tag of the length this course uses
commitResults.messageBody:
A card cuts a tag at twelve characters, which cuts the tags the
product is for: "attendance-low" and "needs-consult" both come out
with their ends missing, and a reader cannot tell one cut tag from
another. The count was picked to keep chips narrow, but how many
chips a card shows is decided by the row, not by this, so a longer
count costs a chip on a narrow card rather than breaking the line.

Let's cut at sixteen, which shows an ordinary tag whole.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '164-add-a-summary-sidebar' into 165-colour-the-command-line
Merge branch '163-redesign-the-student-card' into 164-add-a-summary-sidebar
Keep the reply visible when it is selected
commitResults.messageBody:
Hiding the command field's own selection, so that the coloured copy
behind it is what shows, also hid the reply area's: it draws both the
band and the text of a selection in nothing, so clicking the reply and
pressing Ctrl+A makes it disappear. The reply has no copy behind it;
it is the thing being read.

Let's leave the reply its own selection, and hide one only where
something else draws it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Check nothing hides its own text when selected
commitResults.messageBody:
A rule that draws both the band and the text of a selection in nothing
makes what it holds disappear the moment it is selected, which is what
selecting it to copy it does first. One such rule is wanted, on the
command field, whose text is carried by a copy behind it; anywhere
else it is a mistake, and one was made.

Let's check that the command line is the only place that does it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '162-dress-the-window-in-the-products-theme' into 163-redesign-the-student-card
Keep room on a card's line for a count of its tags
commitResults.messageBody:
The first line of a card keeps a flat seventy pixels for the tags,
which is room for one chip and nothing else, so a card with a long
name or a follow-up pill shows one tag and says nothing about the
others: a flagged "Bartholomew Montgomery…" shows "attendance-l…"
alone while two tags are hidden. A chip the row cuts also loses its
hover text, because only a chip cut by the character limit is given
one, so "attendance-low" beside a long name reads as "attendan…" with
nothing to say what it was.

The checks could not see either: the helper that lists what a row
shows skipped anything drawn outside the row, so a count drawn half
off the edge read as no count at all.

Let's keep room for a chip and a count, name whatever the row cut as
well as whatever the limit cut, and let a chip drawn outside the row
fail the check that lists them.

commitResults.messageTitle: Draw the copy where a field draws its own text
commitResults.messageBody:
A text field insets its text by half a caret's width at each edge, so
that a caret at either end is drawn rather than cut in half. The copy
over it was drawn flush, which puts the two a pixel apart: a click
within a pixel of a character's middle lands on the one beside it.
The copy also pulled its offset back into range whenever the command
got shorter, which a field does not do, so cutting eight characters
from the end left the two eight characters apart.

Let's draw the copy, the caret and the band at the inset the field
uses, keep the line still while the caret is in view, and say in the
Developer Guide what the check between the colouring and the parser
does and does not compare.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say where the window's smallest width comes from
commitResults.messageBody:
The window may not be made narrower than 490, and nothing anywhere
says why that number: a reader has to measure the panel and the list
to find out, and would not know the check that guards it exists. The
panel also cuts a tag two characters longer than a card's chips do,
with nothing to say why they differ.

Let's say both where they are set.

Check the fixed cut where the line has room for it
commitResults.messageBody:
Keeping room on a card's line for a count of the tags it left out
takes that room from the name, so the width at which the name starts
to give way has moved up. The check on the name's fixed cut still runs
at the width a default window gives a card, where in the runner's font
the name now gives way, and it fails there.

Let's check the fixed cut at widths where the line has room for all
three in any font, and leave the narrow case to the check that covers
it.

Leave the sidebar's styling to the sidebar
commitResults.messageBody:
The rule that elides a value too long for its row names a class the
summary panel uses, on a branch where no panel exists: it styles
nothing here, and a reader meets a class they cannot find.

Let's name only what this branch draws.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch '163-redesign-the-student-card' into 164-add-a-summary-sidebar
Let the sidebar inherit the window's typeface
commitResults.messageBody:
The panel's rows name a list of font families of their own, which is
the thing the window stopped doing: JavaFX reads only the first of a
list and falls back to the system font, so these rows are written in
neither the families they name nor the one the window chose. The rule
that elides a value too long for its row also names the panel's class
from the branch that draws cards, where no panel exists.

Let's let the panel inherit the family the window chose, and elide its
rows where the panel itself is styled.

commitResults.messageTitle: Check no stylesheet names a list of font families
commitResults.messageBody:
The window stopped naming lists of font families, because JavaFX reads
only the first and falls back to the system font rather than trying
the next, and chooses the family against what the machine has instead.
Nothing stops a later rule naming a list again, and one did.

Let's check every stylesheet the window loads.

How much of the help window is frame rather than scene is asked only
through the window itself, so three of its four answers are never
checked: a window not yet shown, a scene not yet sized, and a scene
somehow wider than the window around it.

Let's ask it directly for each.

commitResults.messageTitle: Check a reply that arrives before a width to wrap at
commitResults.messageBody:
The area falls back to the breaks a reply was written with until it
has been given a width to wrap at, and nothing checks that: a reply
wrapped at no width would come out as a row for every word, up to the
six the area grows to.

Check the one tag a row has no space for
commitResults.messageBody:
A row with a single tag and no space for it has nothing to count, so
the whole row goes to the chip, cut to whatever is left. That is the
one way through this row nothing checks.

Let a test show a window without stopping the toolkit
commitResults.messageBody:
Showing a window in a test wedged every test after it, which I took
for a limit of the toolkit and wrote off as untestable. It is not:
JavaFX shuts itself down when the last window closes, and runs nothing
more after that, so the tests that followed waited on a thread that
had gone. Telling it not to exit costs one line.

Let's say so where the toolkit is started, and check what showing the
help window does: that it is sized to what it draws once there is a
frame to measure, and that it stops showing when hidden.

Make the theme's own checks hold on their own branch
commitResults.messageBody:
Three checks here are weaker than they read. The one on hidden
selections exempts a selector that only the branch colouring the
command line adds, so on this branch it exempts nothing and says it
does. The one on font families misses a space before the colon, the
shorthand that sets a family among other things, and a last
declaration with no semicolon after it. The one on a reply arriving
before anything is drawn sets a wrapping width of nothing, which
JavaFX reads as "do not wrap", so it never reaches the fallback and
passes with the fallback removed.

The window being shown also arrives at its size a moment later on
Windows than on Linux, so the help window measured a frame that was
not yet there.

Let's check that nothing here hides a selection, catch a family
however it is written, reach the fallback through an area with no
skin, measure the frame again once the window has settled, and start
the toolkit from one place rather than five.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep a few letters of the name on every card
commitResults.messageBody:
Keeping room on a card's line for a count of the tags it left out
takes that room from the name, and on the narrowest window the
product allows a flagged student with two tags draws a name of just
an ellipsis. A name a reader cannot make out at all says less about
the student than a tag count they cannot see.

The width a check calls the default is also the window's minimum
rather than its default: a default window gives a card about 546,
where 490 gives one about 298.

Let's keep a few letters of the name whatever else the line holds,
and where that leaves no room for a chip beside the count, say how
many tags there are rather than showing a sliver of one.

Read where the field draws its text, not guess it
commitResults.messageBody:
A field scrolls by rules that differ between typing, deleting,
cutting and undoing. Each rule worked out again here has been right
for some of those and wrong for the rest: the latest one holds the
line still whenever the caret is in view, which is right for a cut
and wrong for a backspace, a delete, a word delete and typing over a
selection, and clicks after those land one, three, seven and fifteen
characters from where they were aimed.

The field already knows where it draws its text. It is one lookup
away, and it cannot be out of step with itself.

Let's read it from the field, drop the rules this guessed at, and
compare the copy with the field's own text node across each kind of
edit rather than with a model of it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Drop the checks that only tested the old model
commitResults.messageBody:
Five checks here measure the copy against the rules this used to
guess the field's scrolling by. The field owns that now, so they
measure nothing of the product: they pass on a machine where the
field happens to take focus and so scrolls, and fail on the runner
where it does not. What they were for is covered by the check that
compares the copy with the field's own text node across each kind of
edit.

commitResults.messageTitle: Pick the field's text node out by what it holds
commitResults.messageBody:
An empty line shows its prompt, which the field draws in a node of
the same kind as the one it draws a command in, so asking for the
node by kind alone can find the prompt instead. Nothing checked an
empty line, or a box that has never been in a window.

Let's pick out the node whose text is the command, and check both.

commitResults.messageTitle: Measure the caret's advance, not its distance from the edge
commitResults.messageBody:
The check that the caret keeps step with each character compares
where it is against the number of characters typed, which holds only
while the caret starts at nothing. It is centred on the point it
marks and the field insets its text, so it starts a pixel to one
side, and the check fails on the runners where that pixel lands
differently.

Let's compare the advance from one character to the next, which is
what the check is about.

commitResults.messageTitle: Drop a guard against a width that cannot arrive
commitResults.messageBody:
The area falls back to the breaks a reply was written with when there
is nothing drawn to ask where it wrapped, and also when what is drawn
reports a wrapping width of nothing. The second never happens once
there is something drawn, and would give the same answer if it did:
JavaFX reads a width of nothing as "do not wrap", which gives the
lines the reply was written with.
