Set the application version to v1.3
commitResults.messageBody:
The version the application reports is V0.5.1, the version of the
AddressBook it was forked from. The first product release would carry
that number: the line the log opens every run with names a version
this product never had, and a User reporting a problem would name it
too.

Let's set it to the version being released.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the tp-git skill
commitResults.messageBody:
AGENTS.md states the se-edu Git conventions and the course's branch
rules, but an agent applying them has to work out the order of steps
itself each time, and a slip such as an amended or force-pushed
commit cannot be undone once it is published.

Let's add the tp-git skill, which turns those rules into the steps to
follow before a commit, a new branch, a PR and a merge.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the tp-triage skill
commitResults.messageBody:
Issues need a type, priority, severity and milestone, and severity is
where teams drift: High and VeryLow are much narrower than they read.

Let's add the tp-triage skill, which holds the label meanings, the
course's rules of thumb for severity, and the gh command for opening
an issue the way the tracker expects.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the tp-review skill
commitResults.messageBody:
PR reviews are graded on their phrasing as much as on what they
catch, and the se-edu rubric for both is spread over several pages.

Let's add the tp-review skill, which gathers what to check for a
complete PR and how to phrase review comments and replies to them.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the tp-feature skill
commitResults.messageBody:
A user-facing change in TAB has to touch the parser, the command, the
model, storage, tests, the User Guide's section and command summary,
and the Developer Guide's manual-testing appendix. Missing one leaves
the product, tests and guides out of step, which the course counts as
a bug.

Let's add the tp-feature skill, which lists every place a new or
changed command, option or field has to reach.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the tp-release skill
commitResults.messageBody:
A release needs a version bump, a JAR smoke-tested from an empty
folder, release notes against AB3, a tag, the GitHub release and the
milestone closed, and the steps are easy to do out of order.

Let's add the tp-release skill, which walks through a release from
v1.3 onward in that order.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the tp-style skill
commitResults.messageBody:
Checkstyle enforces layout and the presence of Javadoc, but much of
what is graded as code quality it cannot see: misleading names, long
methods, deep nesting, magic numbers, test names, and the se-edu
Markdown and PlantUML conventions in the guides.

Let's add the tp-style skill with its two rulebooks, one for Java and
one for documentation. It runs the mechanical checks first and then
hands the judgement checks to two review agents.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the review agents tp-style uses
commitResults.messageBody:
The tp-style skill hands Java and documentation to two read-only
review agents, which are not yet in the repo, so the skill cannot run
on another member's machine.

Let's add tp-style-code and tp-style-docs, pointing them at the
rulebooks in .claude/skills/tp-style rather than a home folder.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a headless harness for driving a tP's Logic
commitResults.messageBody:
Finding bugs in a tP before a release, or in another team's during PE,
means running hundreds of commands and data files against the JAR. In
the GUI that is slow, and it is hard to tell a crash or a hang from a
refusal, or to replay exactly what was typed.

Let's add the tp-bughunt skill's harness and scripts: TpHarness drives
an AB3-derived JAR's Logic line by line and prints a verdict for each
command, sandbox-run.sh runs a JAR with no network and its own home
folder, poclib.py lets a report carry a runnable proof of concept, and
bucket.py and report-index.py split a sweep by source file and index
its reports.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the bug-hunt checklists and PE rules
commitResults.messageBody:
A bug hunt is only worth the time if it finds what the PE counts and
reports it in a form that survives the receiving team's rebuttal: in
scope, reproduced, one bug per report, with a severity the course's
narrow definitions support.

Let's add the tp-bughunt references: a summary of the PE rules, a
threat model for what counts as a finding, checklists for command
inputs, data files and the environment, source-code sharp edges and
the UG/DG, how to confirm a finding in the GUI on a private display,
and the candidate and report formats.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the tp-bughunt skill
commitResults.messageBody:
The harness, scripts and checklists for a bug hunt need an order to
run in: set-up and smoke test, a feature map every agent shares,
probes in parallel, adversarial verification, GUI confirmation and
the reports. A sweep mode instead splits every source file into
buckets of five and triages each report it finds.

Let's add the tp-bughunt skill that runs those steps, for PE and PE-D
and for our own tP before a release.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add the agents tp-bughunt uses
commitResults.messageBody:
The tp-bughunt skill hands its probes, verification, per-bucket
sweeps and triage to eight subagents, which are not yet in the repo,
so the skill cannot run on another member's machine.

Let's add them, taking the skill's directory as an absolute path from
the orchestrator rather than from a home folder, since they work in a
folder outside the repo.

commitResults.messageTitle: Point AGENTS.md at the shared skills
commitResults.messageBody:
AGENTS.md states the team's conventions, but does not say that
.claude/skills/ holds workflows that apply them, so a member or an
agent reading it has no reason to look there, and a convention can
change here without the skill that applies it following.

Let's list each skill with what it is for, and ask that a change to a
convention update its skill in the same PR.

commitResults.messageTitle: Have bug-hunt agents write their files with Bash
commitResults.messageBody:
The bug-hunt agents deliver their findings as Markdown files: reports,
triage verdicts, candidates and unconfirmed lists. The Write tool can
refuse Markdown report files from a subagent, and in the v1.3 sweep it
did so for about half the bucket agents. Those agents then returned
their reports as text, which the orchestrator had to save by hand, and
nothing in the skill told it to check for them.

Let's have every agent write these files with Bash, return a file's
contents only when no tool can write it, and have the orchestrator
check for missing files and save returned ones before indexing.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep each bug-hunt agent to its own display
commitResults.messageBody:
Bucket and triage agents confirm GUI findings in parallel, and they
share the session's scratch directory and /tmp. In the v1.3 sweep, two
triagers saved GUI scripts under the same name there, so one agent's
script typed a command into another agent's app on that agent's
display, and the other agent had to relaunch and retake its
screenshots.

Let's give each agent a display number of its own, have it keep its
GUI scripts and screenshots under its own run directory, and have it
stop only the processes it started.

commitResults.messageTitle: Set or clear follow-up explicitly in edit #146 (#211)
commitResults.messageBody:
Repeating `edit 1 --follow-up` toggles a student's follow-up status, so the same request undoes itself.

Let's make edit set follow-up with --follow-up (-f) and clear it with
--no-follow-up (-nf), preserving the status when both are omitted and
rejecting contradictory options before any data changes.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'master' into 151-replace-ui-mockup-with-screenshot
Capture the screenshot with TAB in use
commitResults.messageBody:
The screenshot captures TAB at rest, so the command box holds only its
placeholder and nothing sits above the student list. Three of the parts
a reader most wants to see therefore go unshown: the colours the command
line gives a command as it is typed, the reply the app gives back, and
the way a card looks once it is picked out.

The mockup it replaces showed all three, which is why it read as a
product shot rather than an empty window.

Let's capture the same scene from the running app instead: an add
command typed into the box with its colours, the reply from the add that
ran before it, three students carrying the follow-up marker, and the new
student's card selected. Say in the User Guide that the picture shows
TAB in use, so that a reader does not expect a typed command on a fresh
launch.

commitResults.messageTitle: Replace the UI mockup with a current screenshot #151 (#212)
Merge master into 145-see-record-after-changing-it
commitResults.messageBody:
The NUS Student ID work and the explicit follow-up options have landed on
master since this branch was cut, and both touch what this branch
changes. Three files needed a decision:

- UserGuide.md: master describes the NUS Student ID and the explicit
  set/clear of follow-up in the same sentence this branch extends. Both
  readings are kept, master's list of what is saved at once followed by
  this branch's sentence on what the command result shows.
- DeveloperGuide.md: both sides open a new section at the same point in
  the manual-testing appendix. Both are kept, with "Adding a student"
  ahead of "NUS Student IDs" so the appendix reads add, then IDs, then
  edit.
- EditCommandTest.java: both sides add tests at the same point, and
  master renames the follow-up test it sits next to. All six tests are
  kept under master's name for the renamed one.

Four tests then disagreed across the two changes, each asserting a
message the other side had altered. Master's two expect the empty
"Tags: " label this branch removes, and this branch's two predate the
NUS Student ID that master gives Alice in TypicalStudents. Let's correct
all four expectations rather than weaken either change.

commitResults.messageTitle: TAB-115: As a teaching assistant I can see a record after changing it #145 (#205)
Merge master into 149-long-name-value-options
commitResults.messageBody:
The record feedback work and the new screenshot have landed on master
since this branch last took it, and the manual-testing appendix gained a
section at the same point as this branch adds one.

Both sections are kept: "Adding a student" from master, then "Long
value-option names" from this branch, so the appendix runs add, then the
long names, then the NUS Student IDs.

Nothing else disagreed. The edit usage text already carries both the
--no-follow-up parameter from master and the alias summary derived here,
because this branch took master once after that change landed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Derive follow-up aliases in the edit usage text
commitResults.messageBody:
The edit usage message writes the follow-up aliases out by hand, as
"(alias -f)" and "(alias -nf)", while every other option in the message
takes its spellings from the flag that defines them. The sentence can
therefore name an alias the parser no longer accepts, which is the
problem the marker summary was added to remove.

Let's build the sentence from the markers as well, so the message reads
"--follow-up/-f sets follow-up and --no-follow-up/-nf clears it" in the
same shape as the add message, and pin it with a test that fails if
either name goes back to being written out.

commitResults.messageTitle: Edit usage text writes the follow-up aliases out by hand #215 (#216)
commitResults.messageBody:
The edit usage text names the follow-up aliases by hand, so it can
drift from the spellings the parser accepts.

Let's build that sentence from each flag's marker summary, as the
rest of both usage messages already does.

commitResults.messageTitle: Restore the master merge on the student count branch
commitResults.messageBody:
Reverting the merge of master undoes every change master carried at the
time, so the branch no longer holds the NUS Student ID field, the
explicit follow-up options, or anything else that had landed. Git still
records that merge, so it treats those changes as already present and
will not bring them back on the next merge. Merging this branch into
master as it stands would therefore delete NusStudentId.java and drop
the --no-follow-up option, with no conflict to warn a reviewer.

Let's revert that revert, so the branch holds master's content again and
a later merge behaves as git's history says it should.

This reverts commit 9bd8e9566dc77a1a4a9ec6fd87fdb2d8d2be5bbf.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge master into 142-see-count-of-students
commitResults.messageBody:
Master has moved on since this branch last held its content, gaining the
long value-option names, the record feedback and the current screenshot.

One file disagreed. Messages.java needs the StringUtil import this
branch adds for the plural suffix, while master dropped the Flag import
when the duplicate-flag message moved to naming markers as strings. The
merged file keeps the first and leaves out the second, which nothing
references any more.

commitResults.messageTitle: Report the list count without a plural-only "all"
commitResults.messageBody:
The list feedback says "Listed all 2 students." but "Listed 1 student.",
so the word "all" appears only when more than one student is shown, even
though list always clears the filter and shows all of them either way.
Holding three messages apart also keeps the one place in this branch
that spells a plural out by hand, beside the helper added for it.

Let's report the count the way find does, leaving "all" out, so one
message built from the plural suffix covers every count and the two
commands read alike.

The manual-test prerequisite is reworded as a state rather than an
action, because the section above it leaves the book empty and running
clear again answers that there is nothing to clear.

The find test that restates MessagesTest goes as well. Its last
assertion formats the same constant the method under test formats, so
it holds for any wording and cannot fail.

commitResults.messageTitle: TAB-150: As a teaching assistant I can see a count of my students #142 (#204)
Correct two guide claims the product contradicts
commitResults.messageBody:
Both guides describe the summary panel as counting the students in the
"address book". TAB calls that collection the student book everywhere a
user can see it, from the clear confirmation to the duplicate-student
error, and the Developer Guide's own glossary marks "address book" as a
legacy term kept only where upstream code requires it.

The User Guide also says that an unrecognised reply to the clear
confirmation repeats the prompt. TAB answers "Invalid reply. Enter
y/yes or n/no (Enter cancels)." instead, so a reader who follows the
guide waits for a question that does not come back.

Let's name the student book in both guides, and describe the reply TAB
gives along with the fact that the request stays pending.

commitResults.messageTitle: Audit v1.3 guides and manual-testing instructions #152 (#217)
commitResults.messageBody:
Both guides call the collection the address book, a legacy AB3 term,
and the User Guide says an invalid clear reply repeats the prompt,
which TAB does not do.

Let's call it the student book and quote the reply TAB actually
prints.

commitResults.messageTitle: Wrap the find parser paragraph in the DG
commitResults.messageBody:
One line of the FindCommandParser paragraph in the Developer Guide
runs to about 140 characters, while the surrounding source wraps
near 80. The rendered page is unaffected, but the long line is hard
to read and diff in the Markdown source.

Let's break it at the sentence boundary so it matches its neighbours.

commitResults.messageTitle: Parse quoted find phrases with CommandTokenizer #147 (#218)
commitResults.messageBody:
find splits its arguments on whitespace and ignores quotes, so a
phrase such as "Lab 3" is searched as two separate keywords, while
the command-line colouring shows it as one quoted value.

Let's tokenize find arguments with CommandTokenizer, normalize each
keyword like stored field values, and report empty quoted terms with
a specific message.

commitResults.messageTitle: Stop tracking local Claude configuration
commitResults.messageBody:
The repository tracks Claude skills and agents alongside project files.
These tool files should remain local to each contributor's checkout.

Let's remove .claude/ from tracking and ignore the whole directory,
while preserving existing Git history.

commitResults.messageTitle: Cut a quoted value between whole characters
commitResults.messageBody:
Messages.shorten cuts a value too long to quote back after a count of
Unicode code points. A letter and the combining accent that follows it
are two code points but one character as a reader counts them, so a cut
landing between them drops the accent and ends the quoted value in a
broken glyph. The student card counts the same characters correctly, in
a private helper of UiText that the logic package cannot reach.

Let's count those characters in one place, StringUtil, have both the
card and the error message take their cut from it, and say in the
Developer Guide what the shared helper keeps whole.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add an edit distance helper to StringUtil
commitResults.messageBody:
StringUtil answers whether two strings are equal or whether one holds
the other, so a caller that needs to know how near two strings are has
nothing to ask it. Telling a mistyped command word apart from a word
that resembles no command needs that measure.

Let's add editDistance, counting an insertion, a deletion, a
substitution and a swap of neighbouring characters as one edit each, so
that every everyday slip of a fast typist lands one edit away from what
was meant.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test the email length limit through the parsers
commitResults.messageBody:
Email.MAX_LENGTH bounds the address a command may enter, and ParserUtil
applies it rather than Email.isValidEmail, so that a longer address a
data file already holds goes on loading. Only Email and storage cover
that boundary, so moving the check into isValidEmail, or dropping it,
would change what add and edit accept without a test noticing — and
where the check sits is the point of having it there.

Let's cover both sides of the boundary where a command enters an
address: through ParserUtil, through add and through edit, each
asserting the message the user reads.

commitResults.messageTitle: Note the email length limit under edit too
commitResults.messageBody:
The User Guide explains the 254-character limit on an email address in a
tip under `add`. `edit -e` enters an address the same way and holds the
same limit, so a reader who goes straight to the `edit` section meets
the refusal without having been told what it is.

Let's say under `edit` that a new email runs to the same limit, and what
happens to the student when a longer one is given.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say what the email length bound is for
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide calls `Email.MAX_LENGTH` "the only bound measured to
be safe on every stack size tried". A reader takes that as the only
bound in the app, which it is not: a name, a phone and a tag are each
bounded by the pattern that validates them. What the sentence means to
say is which address lengths the guard was measured against.

Let's name what this bound is for — keeping the validation pattern from
walking an address long enough to exhaust the stack — and leave the
measurement as the reason for the number.

commitResults.messageTitle: Stop tracking local Claude configuration (#230)
Find the command word nearest a mistyped one
commitResults.messageBody:
TAB knows its command words only as the cases of the switch that
dispatches them, so nothing can ask which of them an unknown word
resembles. Answering a typo with the word it was meant to be needs
both the words as a list and a rule for how near is near enough.

Let's add CommandWords, which holds every command word and returns the
nearest of them to a word that is not one. A word of four letters or
fewer is suggested for a single slip only, because two edits leave too
little of it to tell a slip from a word the User meant to type, and a
tie goes to the alphabetically first word so that one typo always
draws one answer.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'master' into 171-follow-ups-from-the-email-length-fix
Suggest a command for a mistyped command word
commitResults.messageBody:
A command word TAB does not know is answered with "Unknown command.",
which names neither the word that was typed nor anywhere to look it
up. A teaching assistant who types delte 3 has to find the typo
themselves or go to the help.

Let's name the word that was typed and, when one command reads as a
likely attempt at it, name that command too, keeping the pointer to
help for a word that resembles none of them. The suggestion is shown
rather than run, so a wrong guess leaves the student book as it was
and the typed text waiting in the command box to be corrected.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document the suggestion for a mistyped command
commitResults.messageBody:
The User Guide describes how the command line colours what is typed,
but not what TAB answers when the first word is no command of its own.
A reader who meets a suggested command has no way to tell from the
guide whether TAB has run it.

Let's describe both forms of the reply where the guide covers typing a
command, say that a suggestion is never run, and have
UserGuideExamplesTest hold those replies to the ones the parser gives,
so the guide cannot drift from the app.

commitResults.messageTitle: Explain the command word suggestion in the DG
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide describes how StudentBookParser reads a command,
but not what it makes of a first word that is no command at all. A
reader meeting CommandWords has to take its thresholds, its tie rule
and its refusal to run what it suggests on trust, and a tester has
nothing in the manual testing appendix to try.

Let's set out the reasoning behind the measure, the two thresholds, the
tie rule and the decision never to run a suggestion, add manual tests
for a typo and for a word resembling nothing, and record the published
algorithm the distance comes from.

commitResults.messageTitle: Follow the field's text as its skin re-scrolls it
commitResults.messageBody:
The command line draws a coloured copy of the command behind a field
whose own text is transparent, and reads where the field draws that
text so the two agree. It reads it from the caret, the selection and
the width, all of which settle before the field's skin re-scrolls its
text after a delete, a replace or a change of width. Nothing tells the
copy about that re-scroll, so it stays where the command used to be
drawn while the field goes on deciding where a click lands, and the
click lands on a character other than the one under the pointer.

Let's have the copy follow the field's own text node, laying the line
out again whenever that node moves. The node is looked up again each
time rather than kept, because an empty line shows the prompt in a
node of the same kind, so which node carries the command changes with
the command.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge master into 229-show-a-likely-correction-for-a-mistyped-command
Keep the caret inside the line at either edge
commitResults.messageBody:
The command line draws a caret of its own, centred on the point it
marks, and keeps it off the left edge of the line so that half of it
is not clipped away there. It is given no such room at the right
edge, where how far in a field scrolls the end of a command differs
between JavaFX releases: on the one CI runs, the caret at the end of
a command longer than the line falls outside the line and the User is
left with nothing showing where what they type will go.

Let's hold the caret inside the line at both of its edges.

commitResults.messageTitle: Count a value's last characters as a reader does
commitResults.messageBody:
StringUtil counts the opening characters of a value the way a reader
counts them, so a cut at the front never separates a letter from the
accent that belongs to it, nor an emoji from its other half. Nothing
counts from the other end. A caller that wants to keep the close of a
value as well as its opening has to count back by index, which brings
the broken glyph back at the other edge.

Let's add the counterpart that counts back from the end the same way,
and that reports the whole value when there was nothing to take off.

commitResults.messageTitle: Drive the command line's edits through its skin
commitResults.messageBody:
The check that the coloured copy stays on the field's own text drives
each edit with a TextField method. Those methods go round the skin,
which is what re-scrolls the field's text after a delete or a replace,
so the check passes over states the product reaches and the User sees:
it passed while a backspace left the copy a character out of step and
a resize left it sixteen.

Let's drive those edits through the skin instead, at a wide and a
narrow line and after the line is narrowed under a command already on
it, and let's also compare the character the field hit-tests a click
against with the one the copy shows there, which is what the User is
aiming at.

commitResults.messageTitle: Restore the checks on the caret and the line
commitResults.messageBody:
Two of the checks dropped in 0c1e0aff guarded behaviour the User can
see rather than the model the copy's place used to be guessed by: the
caret has to stay inside the line, where the lane is not clipped away,
and the line has to stay still while the caret moves back within it,
since a line that moves on every keystroke shows a different part of
the command from the one a click is hit-tested against. They were
dropped because they measured the copy against where a field ought to
have scrolled to, which says nothing on a runner that gives the field
no focus.

Let's bring both back, held to the field's own text node.

commitResults.messageTitle: Correct the comments on the coloured copy
commitResults.messageBody:
Several comments around the command line describe a line that is no
longer there. The copy is said to be drawn over the field in its own
Javadoc, in the stylesheet and in ThemeTest, when it is behind it; the
field is said to leave its offset alone when a cut shortens the
command, which it does not on every JavaFX release; the method that
places the copy is said to scroll it to keep the caret in view, when
the field decides that; and the one that sizes the caret claims a
vertical place it never sets, beside a comment about a StackPane the
line gave up. A reader who trusts any of them starts from the wrong
picture.

Let's say what each of them does.

commitResults.messageTitle: Note the command line's re-scroll in the DG
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide says the coloured copy is drawn where the field
draws its own text, read from the field's text node. It does not say
when that is read, which leaves a reader thinking one reading is
enough, when the field's skin moves the node again after an edit or a
change of width. The manual tests ask for a click in the middle of a
long command but not after either of those, which is where the click
went wrong.

Let's say that the copy follows the node, and ask for a click after an
edit and after the window is narrowed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Add a cut that keeps both ends of a value
commitResults.messageBody:
A value longer than the count a label shows it to is cut at its close,
so two values that agree over their opening are put on the window as
the same text. Nothing on the label itself tells them apart, and a
reader scanning a list of them has to hover each one to find out which
is which.

Let's add a cut taken from the middle instead, which keeps both ends of
the value inside the same count of characters and names the whole of it
on hover as the cut at the close does. A value already within a
character of the count stays whole, because an ellipsis takes a place
of its own and would buy no room back there.

commitResults.messageTitle: Cut a card's long name from its middle
commitResults.messageBody:
A card cuts a name longer than twenty-two characters at its close, so
two students whose names agree over those first characters are shown
the same text. "Mohamed Abdul Rahman bin Ismail" and "Mohamed Abdul
Rahman bin Ahmad" read as one name twice. The index down the side and
the name on hover do say which row is which, but a reader scanning the
list has neither in front of them.

Let's take the card's cut from the middle, so that the end of a name,
which is where two such students differ, stays on the card beside the
start. A name within a character of the count is left whole, since the
ellipsis a cut puts there would save no room.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say how a card shows a name it cannot fit
commitResults.messageBody:
The guides say nothing about what a card does with a name too long for
its line. A reader of the User Guide has no way to know that the whole
name is a hover away, and a reader of the Developer Guide finds no
record of why the cut keeps both ends of the name rather than wrapping
it to a second line, which was the other way to tell two students with
matching names apart.

Let's say in the User Guide that a long name keeps its start and its
end and reads whole on hover, give the Developer Guide the reasoning
behind the middle cut and the count it spends on each end, and add a
manual test for two names that share a start.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge master into 173-keep-the-coloured-copy-in-step-with-the-field
Test the middle cut at a count of five
commitResults.messageBody:
A cut from the middle spends nine characters on the close of a value
and the rest on its opening, which holds only while the count is large
enough for the opening to stay the longer of the two. The tests all
pass a count where it is, so nothing says what a smaller one does.

Let's cover a count small enough that the close has to give way, so
that the opening a reader scans by is known to stay the longer end.

commitResults.messageTitle: Clarify that agent skills are local
commitResults.messageBody:
AGENTS.md describes skills as repository files and asks contributors to
change them through PRs, although PR #230 removes and ignores .claude/.
This gives contributors conflicting instructions.

Let's describe the skills as optional local workflows and direct shared
convention changes to AGENTS.md through a PR.

commitResults.messageTitle: Clarify that agent skills are local (#239)
commitResults.messageBody: Clarify that agent skills are local

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge branch 'master' into 172-tell-apart-names-that-share-a-prefix
Merge master into 173-keep-the-coloured-copy-in-step-with-the-field
Merge branch 'master' into 171-follow-ups-from-the-email-length-fix
Name every command a typo may stand for
commitResults.messageBody:
A mistyped command word draws a single suggestion, the alphabetically
first of the words nearest it, and a command word of four letters or
fewer draws one only when one edit explains it. Both rules keep back
what TAB knows: "ls" is two edits from "list" and goes unanswered,
while "eit" is a letter short of both "edit" and "exit" yet is
answered with "edit" alone, as though the other were ruled out.

Let's allow two edits from every command word, as the user story asks,
and name every word equally near the typed one instead of choosing
between them. A word so near that four or more of them would have to
be named says nothing about which was meant, so it keeps the pointer
to help.

commitResults.messageTitle: Check which words the parser dispatches on
commitResults.messageBody:
CommandWordsTest counts the cases of the parser's dispatch and
compares that count with the size of COMMAND_WORDS, under a name that
promises the words themselves are covered. A parser that dispatched
"add" twice and no longer dispatched "find" passes it, so the one
direction the behavioural tests leave uncovered stays uncovered.

Let's resolve each case to the command word its class declares and
compare the two as sets, and read a case however its arm happens to be
spaced or wrapped.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document the suggestions a typo now draws
commitResults.messageBody:
Both guides describe one suggestion per typo and a budget that shrinks
with the length of the command word, neither of which is what TAB
does. The Developer Guide argues for that budget at length, so a
reader is led to reasoning the code no longer follows, and the manual
tests expect "eit" to answer "edit" alone.

Let's show the several-command reply and the two-edit budget in the
User Guide, rewrite the reasoning in the Developer Guide around naming
every equally likely command rather than choosing between them, and
bring the manual tests to the replies TAB gives.

commitResults.messageTitle: Merge master into 229-show-a-likely-correction-for-a-mistyped-command
Read a part-typed command word as that word
commitResults.messageBody:
A command word that stops partway through is measured for edits like
any other unknown word, and the arithmetic answers with whatever sits
nearest. "del" draws "help", two edits away, while "delete" is three
and is the word the User was plainly in the middle of typing.

Let's read a word that opens one or more command words as those words,
and measure for edits only what opens nothing. A part-typed word is
right as far as it goes, which says more about what was meant than the
distance to some other word does.

commitResults.messageTitle: Suggest no command that opens differently
commitResults.messageBody:
Two edits reach past the first letter of a short command word, so the
arithmetic answers "dlt" with "edit" and would answer "do" with "add".
The first letter is the one a typist is least likely to get wrong, so
a word that disagrees on it as well has little to do with the command
it happens to sit near.

Let's measure a word for edits only against the command words it opens
with the same character as, unless the single edit between them is
that character: "felete" and "edlete" are still read as "delete",
where "dlt" is read as nothing in particular.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document how a mistyped word reaches a command
commitResults.messageBody:
Both guides describe a reply that is reached by counting edits alone.
A reader of the User Guide is not told that a part-typed word names
what it opens, nor that a word two letters out has to start the way
the command does, and the Developer Guide argues a case that stops at
the edit count. The manual tests expect "eli" to name three commands
and "fit" to name none.

Let's describe the two steps and their boundary in the User Guide,
give the reasoning for each of them in the Developer Guide, and bring
the manual tests to the replies TAB gives, "del" and "felete" among
them.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep a clipped card name readable on hover
commitResults.messageBody:
A card names the whole of a student's name on hover only where the
count cut it. A name inside the count is cut all the same by the room
its row has left over once the tags and the follow-up pill have taken
theirs, and the label's own ellipsis says nothing about what it took.
A reader can then neither read the name nor hover for it. Any name of
twenty-three characters sits here, and so does a far shorter one on a
narrow card.

Let's put the name through the same width-aware path the tags already
take, so that the whole of it is a hover away whenever the card shows
less than all of it, by the count or for want of room.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say that a crowded row shortens a name too
commitResults.messageBody:
The guides describe the hover on a card's name as the way back from a
name the count shortened. A name the count leaves alone is shortened
by the room its row has, and reads the same way, so both guides
understate when a reader should reach for the hover.

Let's have the User Guide offer the hover for any name the card cannot
show in full, and let the Developer Guide name the width-aware path
the card puts the name through.

commitResults.messageTitle: Ignore the node the field is not drawing in
commitResults.messageBody:
The coloured copy is drawn on the node the field draws its own text
in, found as the one of the field's text nodes whose text reads as
the command. An empty line shows the prompt, and the field draws that
in a node of the same kind which it hides rather than throws away
once something is typed. A command that reads as the prompt therefore
matches the hidden node as well, and that is the one taken: the field
leaves it where it is however far the command runs past the edge, so
the copy is drawn over characters the field has elsewhere and a click
lands on the wrong one.

Let's take only the node the field is drawing in.

commitResults.messageTitle: Clip a name by measure rather than by pixels
commitResults.messageBody:
The two tests for a name the card's first line clips put the card at a
width in pixels and trust the line to run out of room there. How much
room a name wants is a matter of the glyphs the platform draws it in,
so the widths hold on one platform and not on another: macOS draws
"Alex Yeoh" in less than the line keeps for a name whatever happens,
and the test fails there for want of anything to clip.

Let's measure what the name asks for in the font the test is running
in, and hand the line a share of that, so the name is short of its own
width wherever the tests run. The shorter of the two names also has to
be one the line can clip at all, which the line reserving room for a
few letters of a name rules out for a very short one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Drop the detach no node change can call for
commitResults.messageBody:
The copy stops listening to the node it was following before it
starts on another, against an empty line showing the prompt in a node
of the same kind and so changing which node carries the command.
There is no such change to guard against: the field draws in one node
for as long as it keeps its skin, the prompt's node is passed over
because the field is not drawing in it, and a node once found is
therefore the node found on every later pass. The guard cannot run,
and no test can reach it without reaching into the box.

Let's keep the method to what it does.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say which text node the DG means
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide says the coloured copy's offset is read from the
field's text node and that the node is looked up again rather than
kept, against an empty line showing the prompt in a node of the same
kind. It reads as though which node carries the command changes with
the command. The node the field is drawing in is the one meant, and
it does not change, so a reader is left expecting the opposite of
what the code does.

Let's say that the node is the one the field is drawing in, and why
the hidden prompt node is passed over.

commitResults.messageTitle: CommandWords: Keep the class from being built
commitResults.messageBody:
The class holds the command words and the matching, all of it static,
and nothing ever wants an instance of it. Java gives a class with no
constructor a public one all the same, so the class can be built by
anyone who misreads it, and the constructor no test calls counts
against the coverage the project tracks.

Let's give it a private constructor, as UiText has for the same reason.

commitResults.messageTitle: CommandWords: Drop a guard nothing can trip
commitResults.messageBody:
The test for an empty word in opensTheSameWay stands for a case that
cannot reach it. Every command word opens with the empty string, so an
empty word is answered by wordsOpenedBy and is never measured by edits
at all. The branch is dead, and the coverage the project tracks counts
it against the change.

Let's drop it and say in the Javadoc why the word always holds
something.

commitResults.messageTitle: State why the length check sits in the parser
commitResults.messageBody:
A comment in ParserUtilTest explains that ParserUtil applies
Email.MAX_LENGTH rather than Email.isValidEmail "so that a longer
address a data file already holds still loads". JsonAdaptedStudent
checks the same bound and refuses a saved address over it, so the
comment tells a reader of the test the opposite of what storage does.
The reason the check sits outside isValidEmail is the one the Developer
Guide gives further down: each input boundary can then report a length
failure separately from a format failure.

Let's give that reason in the comment.

commitResults.messageTitle: Stop claiming name, phone and tag are bounded
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide introduces the bound on an email address by saying
that `Name`, `Phone` and `Tag` are bounded by patterns of their own.
They are not: all three ask only that a value hold a letter or a
number, and each accepts a value of any length. A reader who takes the
sentence at its word goes looking for maximums that no validator
applies.

Let's say what those three fields do check, name the one other field
that holds a maximum, and keep the point the sentence is there to make:
what this bound is for.

commitResults.messageTitle: Cut a crowded name from its middle as well
commitResults.messageBody:
A card cuts a name longer than its count from the middle, and the row
cuts whatever it is handed again at the end once it has not the room
to draw all of it. On a card at the window's smallest width the second
cut takes back the end of the name the first one kept: "Mohamed Abdul
Rahman bin Ismail" and "Mohamed Abdul Rahman bin Ahmad" are both drawn
as "Mohamed Abd...", which is the collision this branch exists to end.
Every test reads the text the label was handed, where neither cut has
happened yet, so none of them saw it.

Let's have the row take its own cut out of the middle too, and with
the mark the card cuts with, so that what it leaves keeps both ends of
the name. Let's also read the glyphs a card draws in the test for two
names that share a start, since what the label was handed says nothing
about what a reader sees.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say which cut of a name happens where
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide describes the cut the card takes out of a long
name and says nothing of the second cut the row takes once it runs
short of room. The two have to agree on where they take text from, and
a reader of the guide has no way to know that, nor that the rule
belongs in the stylesheet because a stylesheet overrides what code
sets.

Let's set out both cuts and how they fit together, and have the manual
test narrow the window, which is where disagreeing cuts showed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Return the middle cut as a value of its own
commitResults.messageBody:
The cut that takes the middle out of a value is reachable only by
putting the result on a label. A caller that has to know how wide the
cut would be drawn before it settles on one has nowhere to ask, and
measuring a label it has already written to is measuring the answer it
is trying to choose.

Let's hand the cut back as a value as well, and let the method that
writes to a label use it, so that a caller can weigh a cut before it
shows one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep the row's cut from splitting a character
commitResults.messageBody:
A name too long for the line it sits on is cut a second time by the
label itself, and a label cuts at a character index. An index falls
between the two halves of a character Java stores in two, and between
a letter and the accent that belongs to it: a card draws "Alexander
<U+20BB7>田" as "Ale…" with the back half of the first character after
it, at 185 of the 254 widths the line can take. That is the very
defect the card counts characters as a reader does to avoid, reached
by the other road. Reading the text the label was handed hides it,
which is why the tests passed.

Let's have the name cut itself down to the room the line gives it,
through the counting the card already uses, and let the label clip
rather than elide so that a cut a pixel out shows a glyph against the
edge rather than a broken one. The name goes on asking for the room
the whole of it needs however little is drawn, so that it and the tags
beside it cannot chase each other down. Let's also sweep every width
the line can take in the tests, since a width that draws the name
whole says nothing about the one a pixel below it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Say who cuts a name once the line is full
commitResults.messageBody:
The Developer Guide has the row's own overrun taking the second cut
out of a long name, which is no longer who takes it, and it recommends
the middle overrun that drew half a character. A reader following it
would put the cut back where it splits characters.

Let's say that the card takes both cuts and counts characters the same
way for each, and why the stylesheet is left telling the label to clip.

commitResults.messageTitle: Test the name a card is given no text for
commitResults.messageBody:
A Label takes a null text, and CardName guards against keeping one: a
null held as the whole name would reach the width the name reports and
the cut it makes from that. Nothing exercises the guard, so it could be
dropped without a test noticing, and the class is public enough for a
caller to reach it.

Let's pin that a name given null asks for the room an empty one does.

commitResults.messageTitle: Take the hover off a name given its room back
commitResults.messageBody:
The check that names a cut value on hover runs on the label's width,
and a name cuts its own text to the room it has while laying out,
after that width has changed. The check therefore reads the text the
name is about to replace, and a card widened until the whole name fits
again keeps a tooltip repeating what the card already shows.

Let's ask the question again when the text changes, so the hover
follows what is drawn rather than what was drawn before it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Clip the hover test by measure, not by pixels
commitResults.messageBody:
The check that a widened name loses its tooltip narrows the card to a
width in pixels and uses a name of nine characters. A row keeps a
readable width for the name whatever else it holds, so a name narrower
than that reserve is never cut however narrow the card gets, and on
macOS this one measures under it: the card draws the whole name, the
check that the row cut it fails, and the test says nothing about
hovering.

Let's take a name comfortably past the reserve and derive the widths
from what it asks for, as the other tests on this line do.

commitResults.messageTitle: Reuse AppUtil for the application icon
commitResults.messageBody:
UiManager keeps a private getImage helper that loads a resource into a
JavaFX Image, which is what AppUtil.getImage already does. The helper
has a single caller, the application icon constant, so the duplicate
buys the UI component nothing while leaving two places to change if
image loading ever needs to behave differently.

Let's load the application icon through AppUtil.getImage and drop the
private helper along with the imports it alone needed. AppUtil adds a
null check on the path, which the constant satisfies, so startup
behaviour is unchanged and AppUtilTest already pins the icon resource.

commitResults.messageTitle: Name the window's stylesheets, not their count
commitResults.messageBody:
ThemeTest fixes at two the number of stylesheets MainWindow.fxml
names, so splitting the theme into a third file fails a test that has
no stake in how the rules are organised. That count is also all that
stands between the test and a window naming no stylesheet at all,
because the loop that resolves each one checks nothing when the list
it walks is empty.

Let's ask for the dark theme and the extensions by name instead, and
go on resolving every stylesheet the window names.

commitResults.messageTitle: Set the command line's bold weight just once
commitResults.messageBody:
DarkTheme.css writes a normal font weight into .command-prompt and a
bold one into .command-command-word, then sets both to bold again in
a shared rule further down the file. The later rule wins, so the
prompt is drawn bold while the stylesheet reads as though it were
drawn normal, and a reader who changes the weight where it is first
written sees nothing happen.

Let's leave the weight of both to the shared rule, which is what the
window shows either way.

commitResults.messageTitle: Flag a CSS property set twice, not a selector
commitResults.messageBody:
ThemeTest treats a selector written in two blocks as a fault, which
rejects a harmless regrouping of the rules while missing the fault
that matters: a declaration that a later one silently overrides. The
later one may sit in the same block, in a second block for the same
selector, or in a block heading several selectors, and the weight of
the command prompt was overridden in that last way with the test
raising no objection.

Let's count each property per selector instead, so that a declaration
which cannot take effect is named and the arrangement of the file is
left to whoever writes it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Stop a font test passing without checking
commitResults.messageBody:
UiFontsTest guards its preferred-family scenario with a test for the
fonts the machine happens to carry, so on a machine without one of
them it reports success having asserted nothing, and the same green
report means two different things depending on where it was run.
UiFonts keeps the preferred families to itself besides, leaving the
test to repeat the names and drift away from them.

Let's cover the choice deterministically through firstOf, read the
preferred families from UiFonts rather than copying them, and let the
scenario that needs a particular machine report itself skipped when
that is not the machine running it.

commitResults.messageTitle: Read the stylesheet as rules, not as lines
commitResults.messageBody:
The check for a property set twice looks for a rule at the start of a
line and a declaration at the start of a line, and strips comments
only from a body it has already found. Six rules in the stylesheet
head their selectors a line at a time, and every selector but the last
of them goes unread; a second declaration on a line goes unread; and a
rule commented out is counted as one in force.

Let's take the comments off first and read whole rules and whole
declarations, so the check sees the stylesheet the way JavaFX does.

commitResults.messageTitle: Log what a command did to the records
commitResults.messageBody:
The log says what the User typed and how it parsed, and then stops.
LogicManager writes the command text and StudentBookParser writes the
word and arguments it read, but no command writes anything, so a log
read after a surprise shows that something was attempted and nothing
of what it left behind: whether clear emptied two records or two
hundred, and whether find matched at all.

Let's have each command that changes or selects records say what it
did, counting the records rather than writing the student out, since
the command text above already holds whatever was typed.

commitResults.messageTitle: Shorten the merge commit subject format
commitResults.messageBody:
AGENTS.md asks for merge commit subjects in the form `Issue title
#IssueNumber (#PrNumber)`. Our issue titles are often long user stories
or bug descriptions, so 11 of the 56 merges on master in this form
exceed the 72-character hard limit that the same file sets for every
subject, and 4 issue titles exceed it on their own. Merges made with
GitHub's merge button never run our commit-msg hook, so nothing
reports the overrun. Neither the course nor the se-edu conventions
prescribe this format.

Let's keep the issue and PR numbers for traceability, but write the
rest of the subject as a short imperative summary within the limit,
and move the full issue title into the merge commit body.

commitResults.messageTitle: Record the book size an edit leaves behind
commitResults.messageBody:
The entry an edit writes names the index the User saw and stops there,
while add and delete go on to say how many records the book then
holds, and both the issue and the logging guide say edit does too. A
reader of the log gets a different account of an edit than of the two
beside it, and not the one they were told to expect.

Let's have it say the size as well.

commitResults.messageTitle: Hold the commands to the log they promise
commitResults.messageBody:
Nothing checks what the commands write. The entries are read by eye
once and then rest on the levels being right, and find's entry sits
at FINE, below the level the product runs at, so running the line
proves nothing about whether the record is ever made. Nor does
anything hold the three promises around the entries: that a refused
command and a clear nobody confirmed write no entry saying they
happened, and that none of them repeats a student's own details.

Let's listen to the loggers from a handler turned down to FINE, and
check the message and the level of each.

commitResults.messageTitle: Check every field against every entry
commitResults.messageBody:
The check that no entry repeats a student's own details runs three of
the five commands and looks for two fields of one student: the name
and phone Alice began with. An added student's details, the phone an
edit puts in place, and anyone's email, ID or tags could all reach
the log without the check noticing, which is most of what there is to
leak.

Let's run every command that logs and hold each entry against every
field of every student involved.

commitResults.messageTitle: Log what a command did, not only what was typed #268 (#269)
commitResults.messageBody:
Commands in logic/commands write nothing to the log, so a log read
after a surprise shows what was typed but not what it changed.

Each command that changes or selects records now logs what it did:
add, delete, edit and clear at INFO with the resulting book size, and
find at FINE with its match count. The entries count records and name
the displayed index rather than repeating any student's details.

commitResults.messageTitle: Draw the card's parts and the parser's helpers

built from a headline holding a name and a row of tags with the
contact details beneath, which is the arrangement a reader asks about
most. It also leaves SummaryPanel without the UiPart it inherits,
while every panel beside it has one. The parser diagram omits
CommandWords, which StudentBookParser asks what an unknown word was
meant to be, and ParseProblems, which three of the parsers collect
their bad fields in.

Let's draw them, so a reader finding their way around a component is
not sent looking for structure that is not there.

commitResults.messageTitle: Hold merge messages to the 72-character limit
commitResults.messageBody:
The commit-msg hook skips every message that starts with "Merge ", so
git's default "Merge branch 'master' into <branch>" reaches master
unchecked. With our long branch names that subject often runs past the
72-character limit, and over a hundred sync merges on master do.

Let's check merge and revert messages for length like any other, and
add a prepare-commit-msg hook that shortens git's default merge subject
to "Merge master into <branch>" before that check runs.

commitResults.messageBody:
GitHub's merge button and web edits run no local hook, so a commit or
merge message over the 72-character limits can still reach master.
Fixing one afterwards means rewriting master, as the merges of
17 October needed.

Let's check every commit a pull request brings in, and its proposed
merge commit message, in CI before the merge, flag any commit pushed
to master that breaks the limits, and ask for merge bodies to be
wrapped at 72 like any other.

history, so the commit-message workflow runs over commits from before
the 72-character limits applied. They cannot pass without rewriting
master, so that pull request fails the check on every update.

Let's run the workflow in the team repository only, where a pull
request brings in just its own commits.

install creates, and no install creates one: TAB writes the student

only been looked at leaves the folder without a data file at all. A
reader following the answer finds nothing to overwrite and is not told
to make the folder, or that TAB must be closed while they do it.

Let's say where the file goes, that there is none there to replace,
and when to put it there.

commitResults.messageTitle: Accept a command word in any case
commitResults.messageBody:
TAB dispatches on the command word exactly as it was typed, so List,
EXIT and Find alex are refused as unknown commands and answered with the
same word in lower case. No two command words differ only in case, so a
capitalised first word can only mean the one command, and a Caps Lock
left on or a Shift held a moment too long costs a User the retyping of a
command they spelt correctly. The in-app help is alone in claiming that
commands are case-sensitive.

Let's read the command word in any case, through the fold CommandWords
already applies to the words it suggests, so that dispatch and
suggestion cannot come to disagree. The arguments stay as typed, so Find
Alex still searches for Alex, and the help line now tells command words
and option spellings apart, option spellings staying case-sensitive.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document reading a command word in any case
commitResults.messageBody:
The User Guide says nothing about the case a command word may be typed
in, and its section on mistyping one reads as though a capitalised word
is a slip. The Developer Guide presents refusing such a word as what the
design intends, and its manual testing appendix asks only for mistyped
words, leaving a reader with no account of what TAB does with a word
spelt correctly in capitals.

Let's say in the User Guide which part of a command ignores case and
which keeps it, give the Developer Guide the reasoning behind the
decision and a manual test for it, and have the User Guide examples test
hold the guide's promise to the parser.

commitResults.messageTitle: Exempt GitHub's default merge messages from checks

GitHub's default subject, "Merge pull request #303 from
ruihongc/188-strip-invisible-format-characters", is 75 characters. The
default body is the PR title, which also often runs past 72. Yet the
course has said on its forum that merge commits keeping GitHub's
default message do not affect compliance with the Git conventions, as
it ignores them. Our check thus fails on merges the course accepts, and
AGENTS.md asks for a hand-written merge message the course does not
require.

Let's skip merge commits that keep GitHub's default wording, from the
merge button or the Update branch button, and document that the default
message may be kept. A hand-written merge message is still checked.

SummaryPanel counts each tag under the exact spelling it is stored
under, so a tutorial group typed as both T1 and t1 takes a row each,
reading T1 2 and t1 1. The rest of TAB makes one tag of the two: tag
refuses to add a spelling a student already carries in another case,
and find lists every variant. A TA reading the panel for the size of
group T1 therefore finds no row that gives it, and with Lab 3 and
lab 3 also in use the two rows for one group are not even adjacent.

Let's count the variants of a tag together and give the group one row,
named with the spelling most of its students carry, and say so in the
User Guide and the Developer Guide.

commitResults.messageTitle: Show the fatal start-up error without a main window
commitResults.messageBody:
UiManager catches anything thrown while the main window is built and
hands it to showFatalErrorDialogAndShutdown, which owns its dialog by
mainWindow.getPrimaryStage(). When the constructor is what threw,
mainWindow is still null, so the handler throws a NullPointerException
of its own: the dialog never appears, and a user whose JAR or FXML is
damaged is left with no window and no message. The same failure also
reaches the log twice, once as a bare stack trace and once with its
message repeated inside the trace.

Let's own the dialog by the stage TAB was started with, which exists
whether or not the main window could be built, and report the failure
to the log once under its title.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep the words around a pasted soft line break apart
commitResults.messageBody:
CommandTextField turns a carriage return, a line feed and a tab into a
space before JavaFX filters the pasted text, but leaves the other
separators the parser splits on. JavaFX deletes a vertical tab and a
form feed along with the rest of the control characters, so a name
copied from a slide text box whose two lines were joined with
Shift+Enter reads as Siew LingGoh and is saved that way. A line,
paragraph or next-line separator survives but is drawn with no width,
so the box shows the words joined while the student is saved with a
space between them, against the tip that the colours break a command
where the parser breaks it.

Let's convert every character the parser reads as a separator, asking
StringUtil#isWhitespace the question the tokenizer asks, so the box
shows the words the parser will see.

rather than after the first one it reads.

with the quote rule the values use, so add"Ravi s/o Kumaran" is one bold
command word, while StudentBookParser ends the word at the first space
and answers Unknown command "add"Ravi", splitting the line where no
colour ever did. An option written with its value attached, as in

reads a marker and a value there and the same pair written apart is
drawn as an option and a value.

Let's end the command word at the first separator, and colour an
attached option's marker apart from its value.

commitResults.messageTitle: Report student count in list and find feedback
commitResults.messageBody:
Feedback messages from list and find do not report accurate student
counts with clean singular and plural wording. The find command uses
bracketed text "%1$d student(s) listed!", while the list command
reports a static message without the count of displayed students.

Let's report accurate student counts after list and find commands,
handling zero, singular, and plural counts cleanly. Update tests to
verify accurate counts across empty, single, and multiple student lists.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document student count feedback in UG and DG
commitResults.messageBody:
The User Guide and Developer Guide do not describe the updated student
count feedback returned by the list and find commands. Users need clear
documentation of the reported counts, and developers require manual
testing instructions to verify them.

Let's update the User Guide to document the count messages for list and
find, and add manual testing instructions to the Developer Guide.

commitResults.messageTitle: Format student records consistently with cards
commitResults.messageBody:
Feedback for mutating commands uses Messages#format to show the
affected student, but prints a dangling tag label when a student has
no tags and displays tags in arbitrary set order rather than sorted
alphabetically as on the student card. Flagged students without tags
also receive broken feedback with an empty tag label before follow-up.

Let's omit the tag label when a student has no tags, and sort tags
alphabetically when present so command feedback matches the student
card. Update command tests to verify consistent feedback formatting.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document record feedback for mutating commands
commitResults.messageBody:
The User Guide and Developer Guide describe add, edit and delete
behavior without explaining how command feedback presents the affected
record or that optional fields are omitted when absent. Manual testing
instructions also lack checks for adding students and verifying command
feedback.

Let's document the record feedback shown after adding, editing and
deleting students in the User Guide, and add manual testing scenarios in
the Developer Guide covering record feedback and failure non-mutation.

commitResults.messageTitle: Extract plural suffix helper into StringUtil
commitResults.messageBody:
Plural suffix checks (count == 1 ? "" : "s") are duplicated across
Messages and ClearCommand. The repetition obscures the common logic
for singular and plural suffix formatting across user messages.

Let's extract getPluralSuffix into StringUtil to provide a shared
helper for English plural suffixes, use it in Messages and ClearCommand,
and add unit tests for it in StringUtilTest.

commitResults.messageTitle: Sort tags ignoring case across cards and feedback
commitResults.messageBody:
Student tags in card chips and mutation command feedback sort using
natural String order, which places uppercase tags before lowercase ones
and produces counterintuitive orderings such as "Zebra" before "apple".
In addition, manual testing in the Developer Guide lacks a prerequisite
for duplicate student addition, and EditCommandTest uses redundant
message assertions.

Let's sort student tags alphabetically ignoring case across StudentCard
and Messages#format, matching SummaryPanel. Let's also update the User
Guide and Developer Guide to document case-insensitive ordering, add the
missing prerequisite to manual testing, and clean up test assertions.

commitResults.messageTitle: Parse find keywords with CommandTokenizer
commitResults.messageBody:
The find command parser splits its arguments on whitespace using
String#split("\\s+"), ignoring quote marks. A search for a quoted
phrase such as "Lab 3" splits into separate terms "Lab and 3", so it
fails to match exact phrases and erroneously matches students with
separate fragments. Furthermore, unclosed quotes and empty quoted
terms are not handled cleanly.

Let's tokenize find arguments with CommandTokenizer to support quoted
phrases and escaped characters, rejecting unclosed quotes and empty
quoted terms with clear error messages.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document and test quoted find phrases
commitResults.messageBody:
The User Guide notes that find is an exception that ignores quotes,
and the manual testing appendix lacks test cases for quoted searches
and unclosed quote handling. Existing command integration tests also
do not exercise quoted phrase matching against student records.

Let's cover phrase and mixed-keyword execution in FindCommandTest,
add UserGuideExamplesTest coverage for find, update both guides to
document quoted searches, and add manual testing instructions.

commitResults.messageTitle: Normalize find keywords and report empty terms
commitResults.messageBody:
Search keywords only undergo trimming, while stored student fields
undergo normalization through StringUtil#normalizeFieldValue.
Consequently, a quoted phrase search such as "Lab  3" fails to match
a stored value with normalized whitespace, even when typed with the
same characters. In addition, empty quoted search terms share the
generic invalid command format message rather than reporting the
empty search term directly.

Let's normalize find keywords with StringUtil#normalizeFieldValue to
collapse interior whitespace runs, strip zero-width characters, and
apply NFC composing, and report a dedicated error message when a
search term is empty. Also update the User Guide and Developer Guide
examples and manual testing instructions.

commitResults.messageTitle: Keep search active after edit
commitResults.messageBody:
EditCommand shows every student again after each successful edit, so
an index read from a \ ind\ result points at a different student once
the first edit runs. Repeating \dit 1 --follow-up\ after \ ind john\
flags the wrong student, and \ ind john\, \dit 1 -p 9876543\,
\dit 1 -p 98765432\ overwrites another student's phone.

Let's leave the current search in place after editing, as \	ag\ already
does, and document the behaviour in the UG and the DG manual-testing
appendix.

commitResults.messageTitle: Find formatted phone numbers by their digits
commitResults.messageBody:
Phone searches compare stored formatting literally, so a digit-only
lookup misses numbers containing spaces or hyphens even though those
formats are recommended in the User Guide.

Let's also match digit-only terms against the phone's digits, retain
literal text searches, and cover formatted numbers and saved data in
regression tests and the guides.

commitResults.messageTitle: Match follow-up status by whole words
commitResults.messageBody:
The find predicate matches the follow-up flag as a substring of its
label, so every keyword inside "Needs follow-up" such as low, ee, ed,
up, need and fol lists every flagged student. A search for the surname
Low therefore shows the whole flagged cohort and inflates the count.

Let's match the flag only when a term equals the label or one of its
words, ignoring case, and keep partial matching for every other detail.

commitResults.messageTitle: Cover follow-up word matching in find tests
commitResults.messageBody:
The flag tests only checked that "FOLLOW-UP" and "needs" match a
flagged student, so nothing fails if a fragment such as "low" matches
again, and the reported three-student search never runs through the
command.

Let's check the whole label and each word against both flag states,
reject the fragments that triggered the bug, and run the reported
find low search through FindCommand to pin the one-student result.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document how find matches the follow-up status
commitResults.messageBody:
The guides describe find as partially matching every detail, so a
reader cannot tell that a fragment such as low never matches the
follow-up status, and the manual test still words the old behavior.

Let's state the whole-word rule in the User Guide and Developer Guide
and extend the manual test with the reported find low case.

commitResults.messageTitle: Qualify index stability after editing
commitResults.messageBody:
The User Guide promises that the index keeps referring to the same
student after an edit, but the active search is re-evaluated against the
edited record. Renaming the only matching student takes it off the
displayed list and shifts the remaining indices, so a repeated command
can address a different student.

Let's qualify the promise in the User Guide, warn that removing a match
shifts the indices, and cover the boundary in a test and in the manual
testing appendix.

commitResults.messageTitle: Delete: Read its index with the tokenizer
commitResults.messageBody:
The index reaches ParserUtil.parseIndex as the raw argument
string, whose String.trim() removes only ASCII whitespace. A
non-breaking space pasted from a web page or a full-width space
typed by a Chinese input method therefore survives into the number,
so delete refuses an index that is a positive integer while the
character that broke it stays invisible in the command box.

Let's read the arguments as tokens, the way edit reads its own
preamble, so that the whitespace the rest of the parser accepts
around an index is accepted here too.

commitResults.messageTitle: Check every command with a trailing separator
commitResults.messageBody:
The separator sweep walks only the gap between the command word
and its arguments, so a whitespace character left at the end of a
command goes untested: delete refused an index followed by a
non-breaking space while the sweep reported every separator
working.

Let's compare each whitespace character appended to the whole
command against the command alone, across delete, edit, find and
add.

commitResults.messageTitle: Document delete with an invisible separator
commitResults.messageBody:
The manual testing appendix asks only for delete with an ordinary
space or an obviously wrong index, so the invisible character this
change accepts is never exercised by a tester.

Let's add a test case that follows the index with a non-breaking
space or a full-width space and expects the deletion to run.

commitResults.messageTitle: Strip all Unicode format characters but joiners in normalization
commitResults.messageBody:
StringUtil.normalizeFieldValue now drops every Unicode format
character (category Cf) except U+200C and U+200D. Direction marks,
soft hyphens and word joiners pasted from a chat app no longer create
students, tags or phones that look identical but store differently,
while the joiners scripts such as Sinhala and Arabic need to shape
correctly are kept.

Let's strip the whole category rather than the marks the issue names,
so a format character nobody has listed yet cannot hide a duplicate.

commitResults.messageTitle: Storage test: Pin mark-free save of hand-edited data

change. Whether the marks stay gone once TAB saves the file back is
a separate claim from how a command parses them, and nothing in the
suite pinned it.

Let's cover a hand-edited name, phone and tag each holding a mark:
loading drops them, and the saved file holds none of them.

Find: Match digits written with phone punctuation
commitResults.messageBody:
Two close variants of #185 still find nothing: a number copied from a
contact list carries the +, and a number typed the way the UG shows it
for add may be hyphenated, so find +6591234567 and find 9123-4567
report no students against a phone stored as +65 9123 4567. The digit
comparison also compiles its patterns again for every student and
keyword through String.matches and replaceAll, and the && inside the ||
takes a moment to read.

Let's accept a keyword made only of digits and the punctuation a phone
number is written with, compare its digits against the phone's digits
through a named Phone.getDigits() method and named pattern constants,
and say so in the UG and DG.

commitResults.messageTitle: Find: Match a follow-up word by its opening letters
commitResults.messageBody:
A search for the flag matches only the whole label or a whole word, so
find follow finds none of the flagged students, though find follow found
them before #186 and a TA who remembers only "follow" would expect
them. The DG use case also says the status is named "as a whole",
which reads as if find needs matches nothing.

Let's match the opening letters of a word of the label, so need, fol and
follow find flagged students while a fragment beginning mid-word such as
low is still rejected, and update the UG, the DG and the tests to the
new rule.

commitResults.messageTitle: Delete: Name the extra value after the index
commitResults.messageBody:
delete 1 2 still gives the whole usage message, while edit 1 2 -p ...
and tag 1 2 -a ... reply that the value was unexpected, which names the
part to remove. The usage message alone leaves the user to work out
which of the two numbers delete did not want.

Let's reuse ParserUtil.MESSAGE_VALUE_AFTER_INDEX, naming the tokens left
after the index, and document the reply in the UG and the DG.

commitResults.messageTitle: Parser: Strip format characters from the command line
commitResults.messageBody:
A zero-width space or a direction mark after a command word or an index
is refused, though the text looks right: edit 1 -p 91234567 with U+200B
after the 1 replies that the index is not a positive integer, and U+200B
after list reports an unknown command that looks exactly like list. The
value normalizer strips these characters, but the command line does not
pass through it.

Let's strip the same format characters, keeping the two joiners a script
needs for shaping, in StudentBookParser before the command word is read,
and say so in the UG and the DG.

commitResults.messageTitle: DG: Describe the stripped characters by example
commitResults.messageBody:
The normalization paragraph says the stripped characters "draw nothing
on screen", but a few format characters do draw something, as the
comment above the pattern now names: the Arabic end-of-ayah sign and the
tag characters behind a Scotland flag. Read as a guarantee, the claim is
not true.

The delete manual test also reads "the space after the 1" for a command
with no space after the 1, and assumes the tester can type a
non-breaking space.

Let's describe the characters by example instead, reword the manual test
to "delete 1 followed by a non-breaking space", and add a hint for
typing one.

commitResults.messageTitle: Review fixes: Delete hint and manual-test search cases
commitResults.messageBody:
The delete reply reuses the edit and tag advice to put a value after an
option, but delete has no field options, so following the advice gives
the same reply again. The manual-testing appendix also exercises only
digit-only searches and whole-word follow-up searches, so it would pass
without this branch's search changes.

Let's give delete its own recovery hint, "delete accepts one index and
nothing else", and add manual-test cases for the punctuated-digit
searches and for follow-up openings against a negative fragment.

Find: Match a phrase opening the follow-up label
commitResults.messageBody:
A phrase quoted as one search term reaches the follow-up flag whole
rather than word by word, so find "needs follow" reports no students
while the unquoted find needs follow finds the flagged ones, and the
guides state the word rule as the whole answer.

Let's match the opening letters of the whole label as well as of a
single word, so a quoted phrase that opens Needs follow-up finds the
flagged students, and say so in the tests and the guides.

commitResults.messageTitle: Parser test: Sweep every removable format character
commitResults.messageBody:
The parser tests name three format characters at the two positions a
hidden character hides the most, and the sweep over every code point
in category Cf covers the field normalizer rather than the parser
line, so a strip that reaches only part of the input would pass.

Let's sweep every removable format character after the command word
and after the index in StudentBookParserTest, so the test fails if
parseCommand stops stripping or strips only part of the line.

commitResults.messageTitle: Parser test: Pin a mark before an option value
commitResults.messageBody:
A format character pasted between an option and its value reaches the
value itself: #308 reports that -e followed by a mark and an address
is refused with a message quoting a value the user cannot tell from
what they typed, and an ID under -i fails the same way.

Let's pin the add command with a mark before both fields in
StudentBookParserTest, so #308 can focus on the hand-edited data file.

commitResults.messageTitle: Delete parser test: Pin a bare hyphen as a value
commitResults.messageBody:
The extra-token check decides by spelling whether a token is an
option, and a bare hyphen opens like an option without being one, so
nothing in the tests says which side of the rule it takes.

Let's assert that delete 1 - names the hyphen as the extra value, so
the boundary of the option check is written down.
